With the unanimous consent of the house I should like to move the resolution of which notice is given on today's order paper, as follows:
That consideration of the speech of His Excellency the Governor General to both houses of parliament have precedence over all business except introduction of bills, government notices of motions, questions and notices of motions for the production of papers, on and after Monday, February 21, 1949, until disposed of.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS
speechtext:
I should like to suggest an amendment to the Prime Minister's motion. I may say that I have had a word with the Prime Minister about it, and I understand he is willing that my amendment be put to a vote of the house.
The amendment relates to the evening hours of sitting of this house. As hon. members are aware, there has been discussion from time to time about this matter, and it has been suggested that we change the evening hours to permit adjournment a little earlier than eleven o'clock. Last year the committee on procedure which sat, Mr. Speaker, under your chairmanship, made a unanimous recommendation that we change the hours so that, instead of sitting from eight to eleven, we sit from seven to ten. I understand that although there is considerable support for this proposal, there is some objection to it. There was also the objection that a standing order should not be changed without considerable thought.
My suggestion now is not that we change any standing order but rather that we make an experiment merely for the time during which the debate on the address is before the house. The house, having experimented for two or three weeks with a different set of evening hours, would then be in a position to decide whether it wished to continue on that basis.
I should like to add this further word, Mr. Speaker, before I read my proposed amendment. In Your Honour's committee last year I personally supported the proposal that the
evening hours be from seven to ten. There are some, however, who feel that by its adoption the dinner recess would be too much shortened; therefore as an experiment I suggest that for the next two or three weeks we try sitting in the evenings from 7.30 until 10.30. This would mean no change in the total number of hours we sit each day, but would enable all of us in this chamber, including those who must be here because we are-page boys, Hansard reporters, members of the press gallery, and so on-to get home a half hour earlier.
Had I felt that there was strong objection to an amendment being proposed to the Prime Minister's motion, I would have merely have put it forward as a suggestion. But the Prime Minister tells me he is prepared to let the house make its free decision in the matter. In that spirit, therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson):
That the last three words of the motion be deleted and the following substituted therefor immediately after "1949":
"Provided that, except on Wednesdays, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair at six o'clock p.m. until seven-thirty, and shall adjourn the house at ten-thirty p.m., without question put, until consideration of the said speech is disposed of."
I think the amendment speaks for itself. If it carries, the experiment will be made only while the address is being debated, and the house can then decide what it wishes to do.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member
showed me the amendment he wished to move, I consulted my colleagues and we came to the conclusion that we would not attempt to influence in any way the decision that hon. members might wish to make upon this proposed experiment of having the house sit from 7.30 to 10.30 p.m. Unless something else is ordered in the meantime, this would be only for the duration of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The words "except on Wednesdays" are clear, because on Wednesdays, as provided by the standing orders, the house would continue to rise at six o'clock.
The position of the government is that this is a matter which should be disposed of in the manner which best suits the convenience of the greatest number in the house. If the

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time this debate
was adjourned I was speaking on the amendment to the amendment, and dealing with certain questions which had been raised having to do with dominion-provincial relations and with certain of the points which had been discussed.
In the course of the earlier discussions I was amazed to hear the suggestion that there was occasion for surprise at my having discussed subjects which were not clearly set out in the speech from the throne. If there is one principle which should apply in the debate on the speech from the throne it is that those who are not supporting the government on the motion should be able to point to things which have been omitted from the speech from the throne. To carry the argument to the ultimate absurdity that has been put forward would mean that it would only be necessary to present a speech from the throne which said nothing, and then there would be no debate at all. Obviously the less the speech from the throne says, the wider the field of discussion must be outside of the actual wording of the speech itself.
The speech from the throne is simply a statement by the government as to what it proposes to put before the parliament of Canada. They are not the words of the king's representative; they are the words of the government. Under our constitutional procedure the king's representative reads the statement of the government to the parliament of Canada. It is then the duty of hon. members speaking in the debate to examine that statement of the government, and to point out what they think should have been included, as well as any defects they see in the statement itself.
Having regard to the importance attached by many members of the opposition to dominion-provincial relations, as indicated in their speeches to this house, it is indeed surprising that there was no reference to that in the speech from the throne. It was because it is so vitally important that I discussed it.
I should like to point to something in the speech from the throne which, though it was brushed over lightly and without much comment, is of immense importance to hon. members of the house and to the people of Canada. In the first paragraph of the speech, reference is made to certain dangers in the existing situation, and it is stated that "one of these is the communist menace." A little later the speech refers to "international communism"-those are the words; nothing more. At another point it uses the words, "in 
striking contrast with communist countries", speaking of the situation here in Canada. Later on in the same paragraph the words "influence of subversive doctrines" are used. That is the only reference, direct or indirect, in the speech from the throne to the subject of communism and its effect on domestic conditions or external relations of Canada. I am convinced that among all the things with which we are called upon to deal, there is no single subject of greater importance than the threat of communism in the world, and the threat of communism right here in Canada.
In this house we have heard statements by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) in answer to questions in regard to what would be done by this government in respect to the trial of Cardinal Mindszenty. Questions have been asked as to what this government proposes to do about the trial of fifteen Protestant evangelical clergymen who have been arrested in Bulgaria and whose trials are to commence nex Monday. We also know that in recent months the Lutheran bishop of Hungary was arrested and is in custody. The same pattern is being established all over Europe on the other side of the iron curtain. In Paris only a few days ago Mr. Selden Chapin, United States minister to Hungary, now on his way home to Washington from Budapest, said:
As far as conditions are concerned in the country I left yesterday I would like to say this much: that no one today, except the blind and the twisted, can fail to see that the Hungarian people are under the complete total domination of a group of Moscow-trained communists whose sole allegiance is to the Kremlin.
Those words, Mr. Speaker, describe the situation in every one of the countries of Europe where the communists have seized power. Today as never before we see the pattern of communist suppression taking its clear form and being displayed before the whole world through the press reports that come from those countries. As has not happened in centuries, all religion, and particularly Christianity, is being suppressed, is being persecuted, is being fought by the communists in accordance with the stated purpose of that vile doctrine, and in exact accordance with the promise of Lenin that they would fight religion in every way they could.
But this has been true at all times. The only difference now is that it is clearly before the eyes of every one of us to read, to see, and to understand. I am sure that there is not a thoughtful person in the world today who believes that the trial of Cardinal Mindszenty was anything but a cruel sham

from beginning to end, and that every device employed by the vilest form of tyranny the world has ever known was used to produce precisely the pattern which is emerging already in Bulgaria. With the trial there a week away, the reports of reliable press agencies carry the story that two of the ministers who are to be tried have already made confessions of their guilt of supposed crimes that are parallel to those attributed to other religious leaders who have been persecuted in the same way on earlier occasions.
Surely no one can be so lacking in a sense of reality as to imagine that these religious leaders of different denominations and in different countries could, under any conceivable circumstances, all have been guilty of precisely the same technical offences in each country, although separated by hundreds of miles. Read the charges that are to be preferred in Sofia next Monday. They read almost word for word with those that were preferred against Cardinal Mindszenty, that were preferred against the Lutheran bishop of Hungary, that were placed before the clergymen who were tried earlier in Rou-mania. It is the same pattern that has been followed through the whole of Europe on the other side of the iron curtain.
The whole picture of cruel and vile suppression of religious freedom, which is now unfolding before the eyes of the free world, follows right through from the murder of the metropolitan of Russia immediately after the revolution of October 1917. Through the years it has been the same; through the years communists have sought to destroy the firm rock of Christianity throughout the world because they know that it is the strongest defence against the evil doctrines that they preach. We have gone through a period when it was difficult for people to realize that this suppression of religious freedom was a reality. In fact misguided religious figures have come to this country, and to other countries, and said that there is in fact religious freedom in Russia today, and that there has been religious freedom throughout the years. It is difficult to use temperate words in describing the effect of such a misinterpretation of what has been going on in Russia. In this regard I am not depending upon secondhand information. I have seen the anti-religious museums in Russia. I saw the anti-religious museum on Gorki street in Moscow, where any visitor to Moscow before the war could have seen it and should have seen it, because it was operated by the state; and it was recorded in their literature describing the things that should be visited in Moscow. It was used for the purpose of
The Address-Mr. Drew holding up to ridicule everything that people who believe, in Christianity hold dear.
That anti-religious museum is not there today. In the intervening years the leaders of communist organization in Russia decided that it would be easier to gain the support of the western world if they removed this evidence of their real purpose. Therefore the large anti-religious museum on Gorki street has been torn down, as have other antireligious museums which I saw there before the war. These were only the visible and clear expressions of a determined effort by the state to suppress religious observance in every way, and to try to instil in the minds of the children growing up in Russia a lack of faith in the religion of their fathers and their mothers. It has not succeeded; the core of religion is still strong there, but only because of the inner faith in the hearts and minds of the Russian people themselves.
What we are seeing now is part of the clear, stated pattern of the communist party in Russia and in every land where it gains power. They are opposed to all religion; but, as it happens, it is the Christian faith that is coming most directly in contact with communism today in all those countries throughout Europe where it has been such a deep and fundamental part of the lives of the people ever since the beginning of the Christian era. Never before in the lifetime of any one of us was there so much reason for unity of purpose on the part of Christians of every denomination, who see their beliefs challenged by this anti-Christian, antireligious force which has spread its power over such a great part of Europe within the past few years.
The Prime Minister has stated that tomorrow he will make some statement in regard to this matter. When that statement is made I hope it will leave no doubt about the indignation of the government of Canada, of this House of Commons and of the people of Canada that freedom of worship should be suppressed and challenged as it is challenged in so many parts of the world today. I hope that from this house will go clear and positive evidence of the indignation we feel, and that on the part of all free nations there will be expressions of indignation more vigorous, more challenging and more effective than anything yet uttered in regard to the indignities which have been visited upon religious leaders in Hungary, Bulgaria, Roumania and other countries of eastern Europe.
But it is not only what we say, Mr. Speaker. The vigour and promptness with which our indignation is expressed will have much to do with the effectiveness of the course that is to be followed. We are only one nation, it

The Address-Mr. Drew is true, among many nations; but the voice of Canada is respected in Europe and throughout the world, and our motives are not challenged. Few voices could be raised which would be heard with greater respect than that of this free nation, which, with its thirteen million people, has come to occupy such a tremendously important position in the family of nations. As a nation we have our own responsibility, which is not dependent upon the course followed by any other nation. Whether or not any other nation is prepared to state its position vigorously, whether or not any other nation is prepared to express its condemnation in terms that can leave no doubt, our duty is clear. We should say what we think of these outrageous breaches of the most precious of all the freedoms that have been assured to the peoples of the world by the charter of the United Nations. That charter, signed by Russia and by many of the nations in which religious and other freedoms are being suppressed, is the instrument under which the meetings of the United Nations take place. It seems to me that if the meetings of the United Nations are to have any sense of reality whatever there is no subject that can be placed on the agenda ahead of the subject I am now discussing, and there is nothing that calls more strongly for immediate action by the members of the United Nations than the barbaric conduct of the communist governments of those countries which take their orders from the Kremlin. At this supremely critical hour in the history of the world, let us as Canadians speak with a strong, determined and united voice, making it clear that no matter what may be said in any other land we are agreed that by every means within the authority of the United Nations, of which we are a member, steps should be taken to restore that freedom which was promised when the nations met at San Francisco and signed this historic charter.
As we examine the events happening abroad, as we look at the evidence of this vile tyranny never exceeded in its cruelty or barbarity in the long history of mankind, we should not only consider what our responsibilities may be to those beyond our borders who suffer under that tyranny today. It seems to me that at such a time we should consider the position right here in Canada, and what we should do with the communists who are seeking to undermine the strength of this great and free state. Many woolly-minded intellectuals still toy with the idea that communism in Canada is just another form of political thinking, and that under no circumstances should we place it in any different category from that of other political points of view which we say should be freely


expressed, no matter how much we may agree or disagree with them. Those who argue that communism is only another form of political thought cannot have carefully examined what the Canadian communists themselves have said to be their purpose. As we have impressed upon us so dramatically what has happened in such beautiful free lands as Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Roumania, Poland, Bulgaria and Yugoslavia, to say nothing of the Baltic states, with their ancient traditions of freedom going back centuries before our own, it seems to me we should examine just what the communists have told us really is their purpose.
Of the intention of the communists within our borders, we in Canada have a more accurate statement than exists in any other country. That is the result of two extremely important and useful series of trials which took place some fifteen years or more apart. In the first of those trials Tim Buck, the then leader of the communist party here in Canada -and he is still the leader of that party- was convicted along with seven other communists and sentenced to a term in the Kingston penitentiary. Following the discovery of espionage activities here in Ottawa and elsewhere, further trials took place, and we have a clear, unchallenged and unchallengeable statement of what the communists really intend to do. Let me just read their own words, and only a few of them; they leave a clear picture of what they are trying to do.
In no field of human relationships have the communists been more active than in that of labour relations. That is so because of their stated purpose. In the past few days in the press we have read of the vigorous disputes which are taking place within the ranks of organized labour in this country and of how those who are opposed to communism are challenging those who support communist ideas and who today occupy official positions in unions in this country. For that reason it is well for us to see just what Tim Buck himself has said as to the purpose of this activity. These are his own words, and they are in recorded evidence which, fortunately, is preserved and will be preserved. I am quoting from a statement made by Tim Buck to his lords and masters in Moscow as to what they were trying to do here in Canada. These are his words:
The political line of our party is to utilize this tendency of radicalization by adopting a policy of developing demands and initiating movements in different industries . . . On account of the position of the Canadian working class it is necessary to develop demands in advance rather than merely wait for sporadic outbreaks. Spontaneous strikes do not generally assume the proportion or the possibilities that the spontaneous strikes in the United States do, because of the difference in the size of the centres

and the industrial concerns. The political value of these strikes therefore tends to be less, unless we ourselves can prepare them in certain industries. The result is that we have adopted the policy of developing demands in many industries and on this basis sharpening relations and developing strike movements.
That is a clear enough statement of what their purpose is. What then do they seek to achieve if they are able to carry forward that first objective?-which, I might say, is similar to the stated objective put forward in a circular recently sent out to every communist in Great Britain by the head office of the communist party there. Is this line just for the purpose of causing friction and dispute? No; it is not. Again we have Buck's words as to what their intention is:
Once we have mastered the political strike, the general strike is but a step. And the general strike during a political crisis is the gateway to revolution.
That language seems strong enough and clear enough. But the communists tell us, while they are still putting on their mild and false fronts, that they are not talking about a revolution such as the Russian revolution or any of the other bloody revolutions which they have stirred up and brought about in order to gain power. But again we do not need to guess what kind of revolution they mean, because the communists make sure that their party followers know the meaning of the words they use, and they have therefore defined "revolution" in their own statements. This is the definition used in their official statements:
Revolution means an historic event when one part of a population imposes its will upon the other part of a population by bayonets, guns and rifles.
That language is clear enough. No matter how mild or how honeyed may be the expressions of those who put forward the communist doctrine here in Canada, that is what they mean by the words they use. Those are the definitions they have given their own people. Those are the intentions they have put before them. What, according to their own words, is their ultimate objective by that bloody form of revolution? Again we have Buck's own words. Hitler was not the only one who put his purpose into book form. Buck, it is true, has not written quite so thick a volume but he has stated his purpose; and in one of his books "What We Propose", this is what he tells his followers and anyone who wants to read his words:
We shall lead the workers forward through struggles to power and the victorious establishment of our soviet Canada.
Let no member of this house or no Canadian laugh at the suggestion that these people are working deliberately, carefully and with an ultimate hope of success, for a soviet Canada. Let it be remembered that in Czechoslovakia,
The Address-Mr. Drew in Yugoslavia, in Bulgaria, in Hungary, in Roumania, in Poland, in Latvia, in Lithuania, in Esthonia, and in every country now under the communist yoke, there were times when the percentage of communists in the population was smaller than it is right here in Canada today. Let us not ignore the reality of this threat when one of the senior officials of the communist party in Canada can run for the office of controller in the city of Toronto and receive over 40,000 votes in the municipal election, coming within striking distance of being elected. Few radicals realize the value, in a struggle such as this, of official positions in local bodies; and yet local officers have, if organized, tremendous power; and the education and training gained by holding such positions makes for local secretaryships, presidencies, vice-presidencies, etc., points of strategic importance, possession of which might easily make the difference between victory and defeat.
These words indicate exactly the course which has been followed in other countries. They obtain official positions of various kinds, and then use these official positions to gain power, and always to gain power with nothing but a very small minority of the population behind them. In this country, as I have said before, we have the evidence of what has happened. We have the evidence which has been produced at trials, and it is evidence given under oath. That is valuable to us and to others.
However, one of the reasons why communist activity has gone as far in Canada as it has, and one of the reasons why communist espionage in Canada had succeeded so well as it had, was that effective steps had not been taken earlier to suppress communism in Canada. I spoke about the first trial when Buck and several others were sent to Kingston penitentiary. They were sent to Kingston penitentiary under section 98 of the Criminal Code.

speechtext:
That section was repealed by the government which still sits on the opposite side of this house, and they put nothing effective in its place. They left that place

The Address-Mr. Drew vacant in the Criminal Code and it is still vacant. Many people, including certain hon. members in this house, appear to have the idea that section 98 of the Criminal Code was an arbitrary provision directed at the suppression of communism. That is not so. Section 98 of the Criminal Code made it an offence to plan or to conspire to overthrow by force this free system of ours. It went further and provided that any organization which has for its purpose the overthrow of our free system by force could be declared by the courts an illegal organization, and that membership in that organization, with knowledge of that fact, was a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment.
Section 98 of the Criminal Code could have been improved and reworded, but it dealt with something that there should always be power to deal with. It provided a means of dealing with subversive organizations whose activities fell short of the very limited provisions which make it possible to convict for treason.
In the face of the words which I have read, namely, Buck's own statement that they are working for revolution, with their own definition of a bloody revolution, with their purpose declared as being a soviet Canada, who can doubt the evidence available to place before any court to show under a proper section of the Criminal Code that the communist party is a disloyal and treacherous party which should be denied the right to organize and to carry on its activities in Canada?
There are those who say that we must not endanger freedom. The very time when freedom is threatened is the time for freedom to be protected, and protected against those who do not seem to understand the seriousness of the subject with which we are dealing. It is extremely important that there be a provision which makes it possible to take into the courts those who are receiving their instructions from outside of Canada, and under those instructions from outside of Canada trying to set up a vile dictatorship here on the same pattern as has emerged in the past few years in so many countries in Europe. By all means, let us protect freedom, but freedom does not mean freedom to destroy freedom itself. We should make it possible by clearly defined, well-drawn provisions in the Criminal Code to have this subject dealt with by our courts in the true democratic way.
I am not suggesting for a moment that we should place on the statute books any statute which gives to this government, and this government particularly, power by order in council to deal with the freedom of any individual. I am not suggesting that power should be placed in the hands of this government, 

and particularly this government, to hold inquiries in secret as a basis of subsequent prosecution. Let us have a clearly drawn section of the. Criminal Code which will make it possible for the courts to find that any organization which has as its stated purpose the overthrow of our free system is guilty of a criminal offence and that those who, as members of that organization, take an active part in an attempt to overthrow our system shall also be guilty of a criminal offence and punishable by a long term of imprisonment.
Let us go still further; it has been stated here that communists would not be employed in secret posts of the civil service, where their treacherous activities could so easily become effective on behalf of the sovereign state they serve.
Only a few days ago in Great Britain several highly skilled chemical engineers were dismissed because of their known communist affiliations. If it is a ground for denying the right to serve in the civil service, then surely it should also be a ground for denying the right to those people to sit in the parliament or the legislatures of Canada. If it is dangerous to have these people in places where their known treachery can undermine our system, then why permit them to sit in those legislative bodies where the laws of the country are made and where, even if only by power of suggestion, they can undermine confidence by their constant appeals to prejudice, and to the various slogans and devices they employ?
If anyone wants to know why communists are so often to be found actively associated with supposedly worthy objects, it is necessary for him only to go to Lenin, whom they follow rigidly and so precisely. Lenin put the proposition before them in this way:
Is there a single class of the population in which no individual, groups or circles are to be found who are discontented and therefore inaccessible to our propaganda? Our task is to utilize every manifestation of discontent and to collect and utilize every grain of even rudimentary protest.
That explains the mechanism of their efforts. They seek the ground of discontent; they seek the ground of dissatisfaction; and then by joining in apparently innocent false fronts, they fan the flames of prejudice. They use slogans which have been handed down from the German, Karl Marx-and which, unhappily, are no less effective today than they were a hundred years ago. In fact, with all the power of radio, and other media of propaganda, they are more effective than ever before.
Unfortunately many people repeat those slogans and that type of propaganda, without realizing that these are weapons drawn from the arsenal of Karl Marx. With the threat

abroad, and with the threat here at home, the highest duty of Canadians is to do all within their power to strengthen the fabric of Canadian life. We are told that the best way to resist the advances of communism is to create conditions in which communism cannot exist. Unquestionably, the worse conditions are, the easier it is to fan the flames of prejudice.
But it is not necessary for conditions to be bad in order to have communists carry on their activities, and in order to have others who are not communists repeating communist slogans, often without knowing where those slogans had their origin. The arguments of Karl Marx against our free system, written one hundred and one years ago and repeated over and over, are repeated now by other than communists. They undermine public confidence; they undermine respect for authority; and instead of assisting in improving the conditions of the people they serve only to delay the effective solution of problems by creating uncertainty, discontent and strife, which prevents that measure of cooperation and unity which would make it possible for people to join in bringing about a solution of any of our problems under our free system.
The draftsmanship of legislation is the responsibility of the government-because there are two aspects to every bit of drafting which must be done. One of 4those is the-legislative, and the other the administrative. The best drafted piece of legislation will be ineffective unless it is properly administered, and with an intent on the part of those responsible for administration to carry it into effect.
Therefore under our system actual drafting is the responsibility of the government itself, in respect of those matters of major importance which are incorporated in our great laws, and which they must administer. The Criminal Code is one of those in which administration goes hand in hand with legislation. Because of that blank spot in the Criminal Code where section 98 once was, communists have been running free here in Canada, and have been doing their dangerous and deadly work with very little interference-except when their activities became so extreme that, [DOT] consistently with the safety of the state itself, prosecutions at the very highest level could not be avoided.
But there is all this other activity going on today, activity which is not confined to any one field. Do not let anyone take from what I have said the suggestion that this is in only one field. Right here in Ottawa, through official representatives of governments, behind
The Address-Mr. Drew the iron curtain, communist propaganda moving pictures have been circulated in Canada and shown to Canadian children by various organizations masquerading under cultural names. I have seen those pictures: they are clever; they are dangerous.
These highly trained men, many of them trained in the school of political warfare in Moscow, organize very attractive-sounding social groups, invite the children in and show them pictures of what is happening in the lands behind the iron curtain. I remember one picture taken in Budapest itself, a place about which we have heard so much, and about which at this time we should hear so much. That picture showed the scene of destruction. It showed all the beauty of Budapest destroyed by the cannonade at the close of the war. It was stated that the picture showed the destruction that had been done by the German army which was serving the cause of the capitalist west. But then in came the communist army and with garlands draped about their necks and with love exuding from every pore they marched along the streets, acclaimed by the population which realized that salvation was being brought to them under the hammer and sickle.
They did not tell anybody that those pictures showed the destruction that had occurred through the wanton actions of the Russian artillery, absolutely unnecessary action at a time when resistance in the city had ended. There had been destruction, but all those beautiful spots along the Danube, the Fishermen's walk, St. Stephen's church, the Golden bridge, all those things that have inspired a sense of pride in those who have seen them over long, long years, were destroyed, mainly by the wanton activities of the Russian army itself. But communist propaganda will use any destruction in an event of that kind as grist to their mill.
These things have been going on and I suggest that the time is long overdue for the government of Canada to instruct every official office which represents any country now dominated by a communist government that if it is to remain here it is not to circulate communist propaganda in that way. We even had an example of effrontery in one of these ministries taking it upon themselves to attack me as premier of Ontario. I am not concerned with any personal attack, but I occupied an official office, as do others in this country. A communist ministry issued a paper criticizing a statement I had made about the activities of certain communists behind the iron curtain and the publication of a letter which indicated their efforts to threaten people here in Canada. Just imagine what would happen to anyone in their coun- ' try who had the temerity to circulate for

The Address-Mr. Drew general publication criticism of the all-powerful government within their land. Let us show these people that when they have official representatives here, no matter how wrong their ideas may be and no matter how foul the system which they serve may be, we do not want any of their activities carried on in Canada outside of their own official places.
Therefore I urge, and in urging I hope that this will be dealt with in the spirit of urgency which it demands, that there be drafted a clear and explicit and effective section of the Criminal Code along the lines I have suggested so that by appropriate judicial decision in our courts, consistent with the great traditions of our free laws, those who seek to impose a foul and evil dictatorship here in Canada shall receive the punishment they deserve.
I should like now to refer to something that was stated earlier in the debate. In his reply to my earlier remarks the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) challenged me to give an example of centralization. We have several examples before us in the resolutions that we have been called upon to deal with, one of which has been considered already. They embody, within the powers dealing with the control of industry, the control of agriculture and the control of currency, as wide a measure of centralized power as any country has ever had in years of peace.
I want to refer to another example of centralization which seems to have escaped the government's attention. It is a very old statement that power to govern is the power to tax. It is perfectly clear that if any government is to have full discretion to do those things that it thinks should be done on behalf of the people it serves, whether it be a national, provincial or municipal government, it must also have discretion over the amount of the revenue which it can raise to carry out its responsibilities. If it has not that discretion then its legislative discretion obviously is limited.
We had great centralization in Canada during the war years. As has been said, the provinces of Canada concurred in that centralization as a temporary measure because the waging of a war, of the nature of the war in which we were engaged, called for the centralization of direction of military production, of military supplies and of all other supplies which seemed to justify a corresponding centralization of provincial power. But it will be recalled, and I want to repeat it, that when the government asked the provinces to agree to centralization of that kind they gave their solemn undertaking that at the close of the first full fiscal year after the end of hostilities the taxing powers of

the provinces would be restored undiminished. That undertaking has been honoured only in its breach.
Let us see exactly what has happened in regard to the taxation with which the various levels of government carry on their business. In 1939 the taxes collected from the taxpayers of Canada, who are the same taxpayers no matter which administrative body draws the taxes, amounted to $915 million, which was
divided as follows:
Dominion government	 $468,000,000
Provincial governments	 172,000,000
Municipal governments	 274,000,000
I ask you to realize the implications of those figures. They constitute the following percentages of total taxes collected from the taxpayers of Canada: The dominion government collected 51-2 per cent of all taxes, provincial governments collected 18-8 per cent, and municipal governments collected 30 per cent. May I repeat those figures, because the position has changed so greatly. The dominion government collected 51-2 per cent of all the taxes collected from all the taxpayers of Canada; provincial governments collected 18-8 per cent; and municipal governments collected 30 per cent.
Let us see what has happened in the intervening years. The year 1947 is the last full fiscal year for which figures are available, and the figures used are to the date nearest to December 31 ending a fiscal year. The dominion government was then collecting $2,452 million; the provincial governments collected $398 million; and the municipal governments collected $346 million. But let us see what happened to the percentages. The dominion government is now collecting 76-7 per cent of all taxes collected from all taxpayers. The provincial governments are collecting 12-5 per cent, and the municipal governments 10 -8 per cent. If it were possible to imagine greater centralization than that, I would find it difficult to suggest what it could be.
There are other percentage figures which illustrate even more vividly what has happened-the percentages of the total amounts collected by the different governments in relation to the amounts collected in 1939. In 1939 the dominion government collected $468 million, and in 1947 $2,452 million, an increase of 423 per cent. In 1939 the provincial governments collected $172 million, and in 1947 they collected $398 million, an increase of 131 per cent. In 1939 the municipalities collected $274 million, and in 1947 they collected $346 million, an increase of 26 per cent.
Let us see what this means. Municipal councils, and they are municipal governments,

those local governments that are closest to the people and which do those things which in many ways are of most concern to the people in their daily lives, have had greatly increased responsibilities in the intervening years. Yet because of the centralization of taxation those municipalities are able to increase their revenues by only 26 per cent. When you consider the commodity value of the dollar you find that in the actual working dollar the municipalities are collecting less today than they were in 1939. That is the reason that so many of our municipalities are now pressing at every meeting of municipal bodies in every province of Canada for a general adjustment of the taxation structure of the country, so that they may be able to obtain adequate revenues for their tremendously important responsibilities without stifling the initiative of those who want to buy or build homes in these communities.
One of the reasons that there are some limitations on the possibility of building homes in many communities today, when the bank deposits of our people are at such a high level, lies in the concern about municipal taxes as they are. If many of these municipalities carried out all the things that they really want to do, and legitimately want to do, on behalf of their people, they would have no choice but to increase still further the burden of municipal taxation. The tremendous centralization of taxing power is having its impact upon the ability of municipal governments as it is having its impact upon the discretion and the power of provincial governments to carry out their many duties.
In the course of this debate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) explained that, while I was premier of Ontario, I put before the conference held in Ottawa figures which it is was impossible for the dominion government to consider, and therefore they had no choice but to end the conference and refuse to call it together again. Let us see exactly what has happened in that respect. We put forward proposals at that conference, and Mr. Ilsley said that no government with any sense of responsibility could have considered them. It is very interesting to see what happens when times change, and when a government seeks to gain the favour of the provinces by progressive increases of the contributions they are making. I made proposals on behalf of the province of Ontario-and they were not the only proposals-which the dominion government should have examined. They should have examined them, and they should have come back and met us again after they had.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question about very substantial payments being made on account of the war; no one would suggest otherwise. But anybody would be far from reality if he suggested that the whole or even the major part of the increase was the result of what we expended on the war. It is true this concentration has developed during the war years, but it is also true there has been a great concentration of powers, and the entry by this government into fields that were not their own. I shall follow my own trend of thought and then come back to that point. That will be more simple, because I want to deal with one minor example, but one which illustrates my point. Under the proposals that I put before the Ottawa conference in the spring of 1946, the adjusted payments on those proposals, having regard to increases in population and so on, would be $235,656,000. That is to all the provinces if all provinces had accepted payment from the dominion government under our proposals in a transitional agreement. The figure is $235,656,000. The actual amount that is being paid now on the payments that are being made to seven provinces under the Abbott proposal is $240 million, or $5 million more than the proposals I put forward at that time. Yet we were told by Mr. Ilsley at that time that no government with a sense of responsibility could have accepted them. If that is so I can only suggest that a proper definition be found of the action of this government in raising the ante as it did.
The fact is that at that time six taxes were being collected by the dominion government which previously had been collected by the provincial governments alone. They were the succession duty, the amusement tax, the gasoline tax, the stock transfer tax, the parimutuel betting tax and the tax on electricity;

The Address-Mr. Drew and the total of those at that time was $102 million. They said they could not give those up; they could not think of it. The only one they have not given up is the succession duty. The other provinces kept urging for further consideration. They got it, and one by one those other taxes were given up. That is what has happened in the years intervening since the adjournment of that conference.
I was asked a question a moment ago, and I want to point out how a great many of these costs could be checked and where a certain amount of care could well be exercised, and why it would be highly desirable to have an inquiry into government administration similar to the Hoover commission in Washington. In a flattering way hon. members opposite as well as some to my left seem to have been assiduous in reading past speeches of mine, to which I pay much less attention today than they seem to. The interesting thing, however, is that throughout all those speeches I was emphasizing a basic principle which has never changed; that is, that I believe under our federal system there should be a strong central government with clearly defined powers and there should be strong local governments with clearly defined powers, all having taxing powers, clearly defined, adequate to carry out their responsibilities. For years I have criticized overlapping as between the dominion government and the provincial governments. I have criticized increased overlapping on the part of the dominion government, as I have criticized overlapping by the provincial governments. By such an inquiry as was urged by myself and others at the dominion-provincial conferences that overlapping could be effectively eliminated.
Let me give an example of the sort of thing that happens when you do not have an orderly functional relationship between the governments. Reference has been made briefly to this point already, but I think perhaps it will illustrate the way in which savings can be made and overlapping avoided. Under our constitution hospitalization, except military hospitalization, is under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. Personal health is under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. The responsibility of the federal government is in another field. In the discussions that have taken place it has been proposed that the dominion government should join in a plan under which financial provision would be made for a uniform health and social security plan covering the whole of Canada. Under our constitution, unless it is amended or changed by agreement, the administrative responsibility would rest with the provinces. But I want to give an example of the sort of thing that can creep 

in where you have not this clearly defined functional relationship, which does not exist today for one reason only, and that is the refusal of the dominion government to carry on these conferences. The treatment and care of the Eskimos is under the dominion Department of National Health and Welfare. Unhappily these Eskimos suffer greatly from tuberculosis. Already brief reference has been made to the construction of a hospital at Moose Factory near the mouth of the Moose river where it flows into James bay. Something was said about the fact that the contract for the construction of that hospital was let by order in council, without tenders being called for, and that the usual procedure was not followed.
Let us see exactly what happened. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) decided there should be a hospital in that area to care for the Eskimos; and no one who has seen the conditions that exist around the shores of James bay and Hudson bay would question the necessity for providing effective hospitalization for these unfortunate people, who seem to be strangely sensitive to tuberculosis because of the change from their original native condition to the somewhat more protected life they now lead. But the procedure was rather unusual. On April 6 of last year an order in council was passed approving a project of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the construction of a hospital at Moose Factory, at an estimated cost of $1,500,000, and authorizing the Department of Public Works to proceed with the letting of contracts for this purpose. It was to be a 125-bed hospital, and unquestionably extensive hospitalization is needed. The construction of that hospital was undertaken, however, at a most difficult point. Doubtless many hon. members of this house have been in that area and know the low, flat islands in the estuary just south of James bay. No doubt many have been on the island where Moose Factory is located and know how soft the water-sodden silt is and how difficult it is to build over it, and what skill and great experience in building are required at that particular point. Here is an illustration of why an effective functional relationship between the governments would be so important, and how money could be saved. They are scattered across Ontario, and there is a large staff with a wealth of experience in treating tuberculosis.

Right from the outskirts of Ottawa through to the western end of the province are these great hospitals for the treatment of tuberculosis, with a wealth of accumulated experience behind them. We are being asked to consider controls over industry, over agriculture and over foreign exchange, in a bill which calls it foreign exchange control but which is really more than that. It is import and export control. We are asked to do this under the continuance of emergency powers. The government have hardly even made the pretence of suggesting that there is an emergency in the real meaning of the word. They have hardly even bothered to put forward any contention that there is an emergency which would justify the extension of these wartime powers.
Remember that these emergency powers are in certain cases orders in council passed during the war. Emergencies are then given statutory effect by an omnibus statute which in turn gives them the effect of statutory law. The only possible ground for continuing these emergency measures is that we are still in an emergency similar to that which justified the passing of these orders in council at the time they were passed. The war ended in 1945, and this is 1949. There must be some time when government by order in council ends and responsible government by the parliament of Canada returns. There is not one of these measures which, if it is justified in the light of events and has constitutional support, could not now be put forward in the form of a proper statute defining the functions of the government, the
The Address-Mr. Drew responsibilities of the government, and the rights of those affected.
There is just a little tendency on the part of Canadians to examine the way that bureaucratic controls are creeping up in other lands, and without examining with sufficient care the extent to which bureaucratic controls are embedded in our legislation right now in Canada. The emergency controls are far-reaching to say the least; and these emergency controls are worded in such a way that they challenge every basic concept that we have of the right of the individual in time of peace to protect himself before a court under the properly stated laws of the land.
Last week we heard arguments that a desirable objective should not be defeated by any constitutional limitations. If these things are so. desirable, state them in statutes; if these things are so desirable, define the powers; if these things are so desirable, give the individual knowledge of what he can do and what he cannot do, and give him some rights to protect himself. It is not enough to say that these people should have no rights anyway. That is the way dictatorship has come in other lands. When any of those who have public responsibility are prepared to support their theories by the argument that the theory is so good that protection should be withdrawn from any members of the community in that particular field, then we are asking to open the doors to authoritarian practices here in Canada. I do think that these orders which were carried forward last year, and which presumably are the same orders which are to be put before us again, should be read and reread by those who believe in the right of parliament to decide what the laws of the land will be and what our people can and cannot do.
Just let me read from one of these orders, and again it has nothing to do with the purpose of the order but with the way it is carried out. This is the provision in the order in council re-establishing the wartime industries control regulations. This section provides that a controller may make orders in regard to-and I am referring to subsection 2 of section 12 of that order-any books or records, and carry these books or records away and they may be held at the discretion of the controller. It goes on in subsection 4 to say that the powers conferred upon a controller to make any order shall include power to provide in such an order, by way of prohibition or otherwise, for any or all matters which the controller deems necessary to the effective operation of such order. Well, now, this is in Canada. It is in free Canada that a controller who has discretion can make any order as to anything that shall be done in

The Address-Mr. Drew order to carry out the purposes of this act, and in most cases without effective right of appeal.
Let us take the order respecting construction materials and priorities. Under section 2 the priorities officer shall have almost any power that any human being could need for almost any purpose without limitation. One of these, just indicating the breadth and scope, is section 2(e) which states:
The priorities officer shall have power to take possession of or otherwise acquire any construction materials wherever found, and to use or to dispose of them.
And so it goes, right through the whole piece. Then, with all these wide powers, let us see something else. Section 5, headed "Delegation of Power", states:
The priorities officer shall have power to delegate from time to time to any person or persons any power vested in the priorities officer under these regulations, including any power involving the exercise of discretion and any order made in the exercise by any such person of a power so delegated shall be final and binding unless and until it has been varied or vacated by the priorities officer.
Oh, we may think that these Canadian priorities officers could not do wrong. But that is a pretty wide measure of confidence to repose in any human being. The fact is that there is hardly a provision in any of the dictatorships which goes wider than that order today. And the only security we have against excesses and abuses is the common sense, discretion and decency of the Canadian people. Of course, they are human beings; they are not all perfect. And there is no one who has had contact with these activities who does not know that there have been many abuses of these very powerful provisions.
Unfortunately, often there is hesitation to take effective steps to bring public attention to them, as should be done. Then, section 6 goes on to state this:
The priorities officer, any deputy priorities officer and any person acting for or on behalf of or under the authority of any of them shall not be or become liable to any person for anything done or omitted in the exercise or purported exercise of any power or authority from time to time vested in the priorities officer.
That means that the priorities officer can go out, pick up any person he likes and delegate authority to him. Then that person, with little or no knowledge of the act, may go out and do anything he sees fit to do; and if he even purports to be doing his duty under this act, there is no liability, no matter how great the damage is that he has done. That is what it means, exactly.
There is an old legal maxim which every lawyer in the chamber will know, and which states delegatus non potest delegare-a delegate cannot delegate. When this parliament

delegates its authority to a controller, a deputy controller or some person he may name, there should be some limitation to the delegation of that authority; there should not be any denial of the right of redress to those individuals who may be affected by the things done by such controllers.
This is only symptomatic of the whole tendency of the government in connection with the exercise of many of its arbitrary powers. I hope members in the house have read the reports of the decision by the income tax branch as to how it was going to make sure that the waiters in this country did not escape payment of income tax on tips received. After all, if any waiter in Canada does not properly declare the tips he receives, there is a provision in the act by which he can be haled before the courts in the usual way. If he has failed to comply with the provisions of the act, he should be brought before the courts in the ordinary fashion, and have the right to the protection of the court as well as being made subject to any possible punishment the court may impose upon him.
But a new device is employed. Officials of the income tax branch are given the power to determine what they estimate to be the tips received, and then to impose income tax on their estimate of what the tips had been to the men or women in question. Surely that illustrates the extent to which these powers are being carried in various fields of government activity. The official of the department, in this and in other cases, becomes the person who makes the order; he becomes the person who enforces it; he becomes the person who carries it into effect. And this is a denial of what we all regard as the basic ideas of the protection of the individual by the free process of our courts.
I do again urge members, and particularly those on the government side, to read carefully these arbitrary powers, these orders in council carried forward by statutory enactment, and which we are asked again now, in 1949, four years after the termination of hostilities, to renew. There you will see the mechanism of dictatorship. There you will see power to exercise almost unlimited authority over agriculture, over industry and over the economy. of our country. Wider powers could hardly be imagined. And those powers are exercised, not under the direct authority of parliament, but under the executive power of the government itself, without any clear definition of their limitations or purpose.
Objection has been taken to the suggestion that this sets up a police state. Well, there are those in this chamber who know how close we came to being a police state. There

are those who can recall something very similar to a police state, and the exercise of police powers-

It is time, and past time, for this free parliament to assert its right to pass laws under which the rights and duties of our people will be determined. The party to which I and those associated with me belong stated its position in this house some years ago, and it has been the position of this party down through the years. They were read into Hansard of February 10, 1936, and they can be summed up in the following quotation from page 60:
The government of Canada is prepared to join the government of the United States in a declaration that their common objective is the attainment of the freest possible exchange of natural products between the two countries.
That is a clear statement of purpose that was put forward then and that has been carried forward to a limited extent, and it could well be advanced today. However, it is being restrained by many of these arbitrary controls which have been imposed under the orders to which I have referred.
There is before this house an amendment and an amendment to the amendment, and it is on that amendment to the amendment that I am speaking. In this debate this house has an opportunity to say by its vote that the time for arbitrary powers has gone; that the right of parliament to enact laws on behalf of the people should be restored; that any legislation which should be continued should be continued only in the form of proper statutory terms and that those things which we are asked to deal with should be dealt with only in the form of statutes.
From the attitude of some of the ministers, to say nothing of their supporters, it does not seem that they are very much impressed with the extent to which these arbitrary powers challenge the right of our free people to be protected by clearly stated laws which can be interpreted in the courts. If that is so, then the challenge is to every member on both sides of the house to say whether he believes in government by order in council or by the proper authority of parliament expressing itself in statutory form. They have a right and a duty to say whether they want the continuance of the snooper state,

or whether they want a return to the free, democratic processes that were themselves in issue in the war that ended nearly four years ago.
The amendment to the amendment presents limited objections to the conduct of the government, and what is stated in the speech from the throne. That in itself might be interpreted as a general want of confidence motion, but it also might be interpreted as simply limiting criticism of the government to those points that are set forth in the amendment to the amendment. I for one do not feel that it touches upon some of the most vital points that are before us, and particularly the right of parliament to assert its authority as against the right to govern by order in council. For that reason I think that the amendment to the amendment is inadequate. There is an amendment before the house which is a straight motion of want of confidence in the government. There is before the house an amendment which, unless someone is trying to evade his responsibility to vote against the government, or unless he is unprepared to vote against the government, presents a clear statement of the issue. I hope that some of those members on the government sidp, who have criticized orders in council procedure outside parliament, will take this opportunity to express their views according to their conscience. If they do, and the other bodies in the house express their want of confidence in the government as they have outside, then the government will be defeated by the vote and will go to the country, as it should, so that the people can restore responsible government in Canada.

Although a couple of weeks have passed since then, I think one of his comments may bear some consideration. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, as reported at page 237 of Hansard, said:
In every country the communists have two great allies, social and economic injustice on the one hand, and political reaction on the other. If we can destroy these allies and build up a strong, healthy, and progressive society on a democratic foundation, we can destroy communism. That should be, I suggest, our purpose and our objective.
I submit that that is advice which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) might

heed, because I think it is well established that, in every country where the communists have found allies, social and economic injustices on the one hand and political reaction on the other have made it easier for them to gain support.
Shortly after the Secretary of State for External Affairs finished speaking, the Ottawa Evening Journal carried a story on housing conditions in Hull, just across the river. The heading is: "Paying no rent, 59 Hull tenants of doomed flats refuse to move." There are pictures of disgraceful housing conditions. I believe that the former Prime Minister, the right hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King), saw these homes every time he drove from parliament to his summer home at Kingsmere. The fifty-year-old invalid, who lives in a single room with his wife and four children, said residents of the rotting, city-owned, frame structure did not intend to arm themselves and barricade all doors, but added "we all mean business."
He was commenting on the fact that they were not going to move out and live under the skies until alternative housing had been provided. This particular gentleman goes on to say:
X guess I am in a worse spot than the others. My wife and I sleep on a studio couch, while my two boys and two girls have to sleep in a single bed. There is not much room for furniture in our one-room flat. All we have are a table, a few chairs and a wood stove.
Another of the residents is quoted in the article as saying:
That is the best news I have heard since I moved in here three years ago. I am looking forward to the day when we can say good-bye to this firetrap and its vermin, rats, mice and cockroaches.
The article refers to still another occupant who lives in two rooms with her twelve children and elderly mother. With regard to her the story has this to say:
All tenants welcomed the thought of moving "as long as decent accommodation is provided us."
I submit that stories of that type in Canadian newspapers present evidence that we have social and economic injustices in Canada. In the Ottawa Journal of December 6, 1948, I find another story. The heading is: "Sells five new homes for $100,000". It gives the name of a well-known builder and contractor who has just completed the construction and sale of five new homes. The article reads:
These homes are of distinctive and striking designs, sturdy construction, well laid out and particularly well insulated. The price of these homes runs over $100,000.

That is for the five of them, an average of over $20,000 per unit.
Some of the said homes have library, built-in breakfast nook, playroom in basement, master bedroom has private bathroom, also extra bedroom and washroom on ground floor. Some have dish and clothes washing machines with drier, exhaust fans and garbage disposal units installed in the kitchens, and many other modern built-in features for easy housekeeping and solid comfort.
I must remind you, Mr. Speaker, that in one edition of the Ottawa Journal we have a story of the disgraceful conditions which exist for these Hull tenants, pictures of which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of February 4, and in another edition we are told of five houses having been purchased recently at a cost of $100,000. I submit that while there are houses being built and sold to one group of our Canadian people at a price of $20,000 each, and you have slum conditions remaining undisturbed year after year, you have a situation which breeds communism. In the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of July 18, 1947, there is an editorial headed: "Action on housing needed".
It seems ironical that nations which can produce atom bombs, develop radar and thousands of other wartime inventions, and send planes circling the globe in a matter of hours-feats which our ancestors of one hundred or two hundred years ago would have thought fantastic-have lost the knack, which those long dead pioneers had, of putting up homes without draining the family's financial resources dry.
A great many young men and women who fought for Canada, who fought to save their homes and to get homes, find it very difficult in 1949 to understand why the nation that could do all these marvellous things from 1939 to 1945 now seems so helpless when it comes to dealing with our housing problem. Last year the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) mentioned that the cost of defence was going up, and that one of the commitments he had authorized was a $600,000 gun. I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) state that defence now is very costly, that every time we take three hundred men into the armed forces we increase our national expenditure by $1 million per year. I think the time has come when those who are responsible for appropriating funds in this parliament must find money with which to tackle our slum clearing -and housing problems in the same way we tackled our defence expenditures in time of war.
When I have discussed the question of housing in previous years I have made the mistake of leaving the important matter of rural housing until the end. Unlike the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) I have not unlimited time at my disposal, so today I plan

The Address-Mr. Nicholson to make my reference to rural housing before reaching the end of my time. In 1944 Professor Arthur, who was a member of the committee appointed by the government to prepare the well known Curtis report, gave an interesting lecture on housing for Canada. In the section devoted to farm housing he drew attention to the fact that Canada needed at least one hundred thousand new houses for our farm folk to replace obsolescent homes and at least another twenty-five thousand to provide separate units for farm families. In his comment he said:
We are inclined to assume too readily that the farmer and his family are happy with their outhouse, their oil lamps, lack of refrigeration and lack of bathing facilities except where provided by a galvanized basin. Of the total farm buildings in Canada (730,000), 677,100 or 92-7 per cent were without bathing facilities and 92 per cent lacked flush toilets.
I want to suggest to the new minister of reconstruction (Mr. Winters), who soon will be confronted with the problem of providing employment for Canadians, that the installation of bathing facilities and flush toilets in 92-7 per cent of the farm homes of Canada should provide an outlet for a great deal of material as well as employment for a great many artisans. Professor Arthur referred to the tables showing the condition of farm houses all across the country, and it is a picture of which we cannot be very proud. I am sure many of our young people have left the farms and gone to the cities because it has been so difficult to get running water, electricity and modern conveniences in the farm homes of Canada.
Of course I realize that this is partly an economic problem. If the farmers could have a fair share of the national income over a period of years I am sure many of them would modernize their homes. But unfortunately the farmers have not been receiving a fair share of the national income, and consequently	a	fair	share	of	the	material	and
labour used in the construction of homes has not gone into farm homes. In one of the green books prepared for the dominion-provincial conference in 1945, entitled "Public Investment and Capital Formation" some very interesting information may be found relating to the percentages of the gross investment, according to types, over a number of years. More than 40 per cent of the farm buildings in Canada were in need of external repairs in 1941.
