The Address-Mr. Nicholson Mr. Nicholson: My time is passing quickly, Mr. Speaker, and I wish to say something about an urgent problem that confronts so many Canadian people. During the dinner recess I was glad to read that the Prime Minister has changed his attitude. I think he made an unfortunate statement about a year ago to the effect that no government of which he was a member would take any part in a low-rental, subsidized-housing scheme. But in Toronto, over the week-end, he indicated that he at least has an open mind. In the Toronto Telegram of today I read the following:
Although the federal government has no intention of becoming a landlord to civilians, Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent hinted today that the dominion may provide additional financial assistance for low rental housing projects initiated provincially or municipally.
Mr. St. Laurent did not indicate in detail what form the extra housing assistance might take but, in a general way, it was evident that he will propose an extension of slum clearance grants from the federal treasury.
His statement was significant in view of the fact that about an hour earlier, he and Mayor Hiram McCallum had visited the Regent park housing project.
At this stage I should like to thank again the Toronto board of trade for the very interesting tour they arranged last year when members of parliament were in Toronto. On some occasions of that sort people who are your hosts take you only to the best residential areas in the city, but our hosts in Toronto took us to the Regent park area, and I am looking forward with a great deal of pleasure to going back to see what has taken place in that slum area since we were there a year ago. I continue with the quotation. The Prime Minister said:
"I believe I am correct in saying that it is the first time in Canada a municipality has undertaken a large scale project to look after the housing needs of low income families.
The Regent park project demonstrates that, when the local authorities really mean business, they can secure the effective co-operation of the provincial and federal governments."
The Prime Minister plainly made a courtly and pleasant bid for Toronto's favour. At another point in his address he declared that: "The city of Toronto has given an outstanding example of the practical way in which governments can work together in the public interest."
"Perhaps," he added, "you will excuse me for saying that there was so much goodwill between the city and the federal government that it overflowed and brought in the provincial government as well."
I am delighted to find that the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition are on such friendly terms that they go to the city of Toronto and together take some credit for the fact that they were even able to work out for the Toronto municipal authorities the program which has been carried on there and which is going to result in about 1,000 low-

rental houses being made available to these people who are living in the Regent park area. I understand that the area where the houses are to be demolished contains forty-one acres. They have undertaken to house everyone living in that area and about 200 additional families. In addition to having grounds for flowers and vegetables around the units, they are going to have about ten acres in park land in that project. While funds have been used from the federal treasury, and while Toronto is one of the wealthiest cities in Canada, yet as a member representing a rural constituency I am glad that Canada has made a start and that Toronto is going to show the rest of Canada what can be done when municipal, provincial and federal authorities bury their prejudices and work out a program to serve the best interests of the greatest number.
I have a few newspaper clippings from across the country to indicate how general the interest is in facing up to the housing problem which confronts so many of our people. The Financial Post carried an interesting story on July 19, following the representations made by the mayors association in trying to get the federal government to meet with representatives from the provinces and the municipalities to work out the details. The Evening Times of Saint John of June 23, 1948, carries a story which reads as follows:
Low-rentals housing plan still problem. The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities today was faced with four choices in its efforts for a low rent program in Canada.
"If our analysis of the situation is correct," he said, "then we can conclude that the outlook for minimum standard low-rental housing for low wage families, as part of the national over-all house construction program, is a doubtful prospect until the federal and provincial governments have come together and resolved a program of action."
The Ottawa Evening Journal of June 24 carries a story from Halifax where the mayors had their annual meeting. From the Winnipeg Citizen of September 27, 1948, we get the following story written by Beland Honderich, financial editor of the Toronto Star:
The federal government's advisory committee on post-war reconstruction recognized this point in its housing study. In its report to the government in 1944-four years ago-the housing subcommittee bluntly stated that the provision of adequate low-rental housing was essential to the solution of the shortage. It said:
"The proportions of the post-war (housing) program which will be supplied through publicly assisted building for ownership and publicly assisted low-rental housing will depend on a number of factors . . . But that a very large and long range program of low-rental housing must be contemplated is an inescapable conclusion from the available facts."
With such a detailed and authoritative report to guide them, the inactivity of the various levels of government is a bit difficult to understand. Equally disturbing is the attitude of acting Prime Minister

St. Laurent. For In face of this report, he said in a speech last November:	. . no government of
which I am a part will ever pass legislation for subsidized housing."
If Mr. St. Laurent's statement means what it says, then the solution to the housing shortage is a long way off. In fact, it is hopeless. For the provincial and municipal governments alone cannot be expected to carry the financial burden of low-cost housing. The cost is too great.
I have also a story from the Halifax Mail of March 28. I have several more that I will not have time to discuss.
I should like to refer for a moment to a section of the Curtis report dealing with the position in which many of our low-income families find themselves. In 1941, in connection with the taking of the census, a special study was made in twelve metropolitan cities in Canada. These cities contain 60 per cent of the urban population of the whole dominion. They went to 834,000 dwellings and found that 530,000, or two-thirds of them, were rented. They found that one-third of this very large number living in rented accommodation received an annual income of $703. The .second third had an average income of $1,389. The one-third who were getting $1,800 or thereabouts were able to look after their own accommodation but for at least two-thirds of these 530,000 families in the twelve metropolitan cities we find that their income was quite inadequate to provide food, clothing and shelter. It is a well established principle in all countries that not more than 20 per cent of one's income should go for rental, or if one is buying one should not pay more than two years' total salary for a house. On this basis we find 88 per cent of the people in the lowest income brackets in these rented houses were paying a disproportionate amount for their living quarters. For example, those who were getting an average of $703 a year were paying $7.28 per month more than they should have paid for living quarters. About 50 per cent of those who were getting an average of $1,389 were also paying more than they should have paid for rent. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the fact that in Canada we have a large number of people on salaries and wages fixed so low that they are unable to buy or rent living accommodation presents a very urgent problem to all of us.
In 1919 a special commission was set up to look into the unrest which existed all across Canada. In reporting, the late Mr. Justice Mathers said:
Another cause of unrest which we met with at practically every place we visited was the scarcity of houses and the poor quality of some of those which did exist.
A number of years passed without anything being done. In 1935 parliament set up a special committee to study the housing
The Address-Mr. Nicholson problem. The hon. member for Broadview is the only member of the present parliament who was on that committee. He has been able to survive three federal elections since that time. Naturally the hon. member was keenly interested in housing problems and said:
As you know, this country cannot solve any problems at all because of its "passing-the-buck" act, the British North America Act; it cannot settle any problems at all, except objectively. If we want to do something in this committee we need to get busy, particularly because spring is coming; and I do not think many of the municipalities are able to go ahead on their own. Men are waiting for jobs and cannot get them.
That was in 1935. Spring is coming again, and very little has been done by way of dealing with the problem, which concerns so many people.
One of the cities discussed upon that occasion was Cleveland. The committee took the trouble to hear evidence from Cleveland, where they had made a study of slum problems, and from that city the committee obtained statistics showing what it had cost to maintain the slum area over a number of years. I am happy to say that in the United States, as a result of the progressive leadership of the late President Roosevelt, they passed legislation in the thirties, when we were paying large sums of money to keep carpenters and plumbers on relief. In the United States they decided that it would be better to clear away their slums, to build new houses than to pay people to do nothing, and Cleveland was one of the places where they took action.
When one stops to consider the wretchedly unsanitary and unsocial conditions formerly existing in these slum areas, which have been eliminated; the ramshackle frame buildings, which have been torn down; and then goes into one of these neat new apartments with steam heat, hot and cold water, sanitary plumbing, with modern laundry facilities, well-lighted and ventilated rooms, good sidewalks with growing trees, green grass and shrubs, assembly halls, club rooms and nursery and kindergarten rooms; playground equipment, tot lots with sand boxes for the youngsters

all away from the noise and danger of street traffic-he begins to realize the fundamental nature of these improvements.
Furthermore, private charity in one year poured into this slum district $490,836 to supplement the city expenditures. Fire protection in this area cost the taxpayers $18.27 per capita previously, while the average in the city was $4.37. It would be difficult to estimate the incalculable losses in physical

The Address-Mr. Nicholson health, social morale and political domination, which always result from slum areas and bad housing.
I am sorry I have not enough time to deal at some length with the municipal housing program in Toronto. Before concluding however I should like to refer to a publication entitled "Rents for Regent Park", a study made by Humphrey Carver and Alison L. Hopwood, which provides a pattern for the Toronto housing association, determining rents which should be paid. They refer to the system followed in Birmingham, where the central government provides a subsidy of $66 a year for each of the families which have been rehoused, and Birmingham provides $22. So that the monthly rental is $15.13 for modern houses. Mr. Carver refers to some of the projects in the United States where they follow a pattern of taking approximately 20 per cent of an individual's income for rent, the balance being paid partly by the central government and partly by the association. In other words, if one were receiving an income of $1,100 he would pay $26 for the smallest type apartment.
In Australia they have a similar plan, where the central government provides three-fifths of the cost, by subsidy, and the state government two-fifths. The municipality of course is charged with the responsibility of managing and servicing the area. Professor Carver worked out an elaborate program which will be in effect in Regent park, I understand. Those who get $80 a month, if they have six children, pay only $19 a month, made up of $11 rent plus $8 for service charges. And if one lived in the same quarters, and had an income of $299 a month, he would pay $62 a month. I believe that is a fair and sound principle, namely, that the individual should pay according to his ability, in connection with these projects in which the federal government, the provincial government and the municipality have an investment.
In concluding I would urge again that the dominion government act on the suggestions made by the association of mayors, the Canadian Legion and many other organizations. A conference of the dominion, provincial and municipal authorities should be convened immediately to discuss around a table just where we go from here. I believe the least the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) can do is to take the initiative in calling the conference.
It must be pretty obvious that these are responsibilities for the federal government. It is the federal government which decides where war industries will locate, which decides that farmers are to get such low 
prices that farm boys must go to the cities and thereby create housing problems in those cities. The federal government must take some responsibility and part in financing and making grants for rent reduction funds and for slum clearance.
The provincial governments also have responsibilities. They must direct the use of the land. They must enact legislation authorizing the establishing of local housing authorities. They must encourage and legislate both for housing and for community planning. They must be prepared to undertake the actual execution and management of housing projects in rural areas and in scattered communities. The municipal authorities, I believe, are the natural ones to establish the local authority charged with the building and operation of the public housing projects. They must take the responsibility for acquiring the land, preparing the designs, the letting of contracts on a competitive basis and maintaining the project in good repair. They must be responsible for the selection of tenants, the collection of rents and the general well-being of the tenants.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first to join with other hon. members in complimenting the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) who moved the address in reply, and the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Demers) who seconded it, upon the very excellent speeches they delivered in carrying out their important function in this regard.
The hon. member for Essex West has spoken well in the house before. His contribution was well prepared and well delivered, in accordance with the standard his colleagues expected of him. On the other hand, the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains had the more exacting task of delivering his maiden speech in the house. I am sure the electors of his constituency have been proud to learn of the exceedingly fine contribution he made; and the ovation with which the conclusion of his remarks was hailed was a tribute not only to a most excellent maiden speech but also to the good judgment of all those who sent him to represent them here.
Most sincere congratulations also are due to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) upon

his selection by his party to assume the heavy responsibilities he has undertaken, also on the magnificent speech which he delivered in this debate, a speech which has been hailed on all sides as a tour de force and which to his followers and well-wishers, both within and without this house, has been and will continue to be a source of inspiration and extreme gratification.
Turning now to the speech from the throne I should like to discuss several matters which I think are of particular interest to my province and to the constituency of Halifax, which I have the honour to represent along with my colleague (Mr. Isnor). Halifax is a city which in the past has been touched by the hand of war. Throughout its 200 years of history it has been closer to the succession of armed conflicts which have marked these two centuries than any other part of the territory which now comprises the Dominion of Canada. Against this background of the awareness of the realities of war there will be throughout the province of Nova Scotia general agreement with the statement of government policy in connection with matters that are in the sphere of international relations.
A large majority of the people of Nova Scotia will have welcomed also the elaboration of government policy in this regard which was provided by the Prime Minister when he set out the measures which this government and the Liberal party consider it is necessary to take in the interests of the peace and security of this nation.
The north Atlantic security pact is accepted, I think, by the people of my province as a necessary and wise precaution to ensure that any potential aggressor will be faced by a united group of free nations before, rather than after, such an aggressor may have become committed to a policy which would make inevitable the outbreak of a third world war. We regard this treaty, and I think the majority of the Canadian people so regard it, as a realistic attempt to prevent the course of our dealings with today's aggressive dictators following the melancholy and fatal course which was followed in the dealings with Hitler and Mussolini. In these days of tension between the east and the west we run the risk of war, but it is a calculated risk which most people agree is one that we must accept and undergo if we are to hope for the future firm establishment of peace.
The house and the country appreciate the excellent maiden speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). His speech was such that I feel somewhat presumptuous in complimenting him upon it, but I do so most sincerely and wholeheartedly.
The Address-Mr. Dickey
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke in this debate on the first occasion for some two hours and twenty minutes. During that speech he found it possible to devote less than one hundred words to the all-important question of external affairs. He spoke for forty minutes two weeks ago Friday night, and today he spoke for two hours and fifteen minutes. It is almost unbelievable that in that time the simple but today expressive words "north Atlantic security pact" are not to be found from the beginning to the end of his remarks.
The leader of the opposition in the meantime explained this omission on the ground that he did not feel free to discuss this pact until the pact itself had been brought before the house. The strictness with which hon. members who sit around him have observed the same reticence in their contributions to this debate marks this as a matter of party policy rather than the personal opinion of their leader. In spite of any virtue which thal explanation may have in point of ingenuity I am satisfied that it will not commend itself to this house or to the country as deserving of belief. It seems to me to lack completely the characteristic of reality which is a condition precedent to credibility. To follow the diplomatic phraseology of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, it does not command respect.
For example, we find it impossible not to ask ourselves how this ingenious explanation can be made to coincide with statements made in other circumstances by hon. members opposite with respect to the supremacy of parliament and the importance of this debate on the address. We heard further statements of that nature this afternoon. It is not difficult to imagine what the reaction of the same hon. gentlemen would be if such a limitation were attempted to be imposed from this side of the house. However, it is not necessary for us to rely upon our powers of imagination. The leader of the opposition, and much more particularly his followers, have discussed, with commendable freedom of choice, the measures and matters forecast in the speech from the throne, with the sole exception I believe of the north Atlantic security pact.

In the speech from the throne reference is made to the co-operation which has been received from all the provinces in connection with the national health program announced last session. Nova Scotia is one of the provinces co-operating to the fullest possible extent in bringing to its people the benefits of this magnificent program. In the constituency of Halifax alone already two country hospitals, commenced through the initiative of the people of small but virile communities, have received assistance through the grants in aid of hospital construction. Under this plan contributions by both the dominion and the provincial governments have been made to hospitals at Sheet Harbour and Mus-quodoboit Harbour. The need for these hospitals was so great that, even before the national health program was announced, leaders in these communities had formulated their plans and organized themselves to provide in their localities the best hospital facilities that could be established. The,assistance under the hospital grants program has been of the greatest value to them in bringing their plans to realization in the form of substantial buildings with all modern facilities for the treatment and care of the sick, thus

The Address-Mr. Dickey filling a long-felt need in these communities. Their pride in their own achievements I know is mixed with feelings of sincere appreciation for the assistance provided through the national health program. The forecast in the speech from the throne of measures to assist the Canadian shipbuilding industry is extremely welcome in Halifax, and the legislation the government intends to bring forward will be anxiously awaited. Halifax Shipyards Limited and other firms connected with the shipbuilding and ship repairing' trades in Halifax are extremely important elements in the industrial economy not only of our city and county but of the province and country as a whole. Through the efforts of both management and labour the capacity and efficiency of the Halifax shipyards were tremendously extended during the years of war, and it has been a source of great satisfaction to all those interested in the maintenance of prosperous conditions in Halifax that the activities of this great industry have been maintained at a very high level.
In this connection I would remind the house that Canada, particularly the maritime provinces, has a tremendous stake in the sea and the commerce of the sea. The citizens of Halifax realize how closely their prosperity is bound up with the fortunes of Canada as a maritime nation. The remarks in this debate by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) therefore call for some comment. I would remind the hon. member, and call the attention of the house to the fact, that the argument he adopted in reference to the difficulties presently being experienced by the operators of the Canadian merchant marine is regarded by many people who know the facts as nothing but communist propaganda. The hon. member's discussion and interpretation of the Canada Shipping Act and his exchanges in this connection with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) were amusing, but I do not propose to enter into any discussion of the statutory provisions to which they referred. I am speaking rather of what the hon. member had to say with respect to the possibility of the Canadian flag slowly disappearing from the seas.
To indicate to the house the opinion held by many people, not only in Halifax but in other parts of the country, with respect to the kind of argument put forward the other


evening in the hon. member's presentation to the house, I should like to quote from a story which appeared in the Halifax Free Press of January 28, 1949. The story is headed, "Communist propaganda floods Halifax and other ports." The subheading is, "Experienced seamen forced to stay ashore while landlubbers and 'one-trippers' get jobs thanks tc union." The story goes on:
In one of the most blatant propaganda hoaxes in recent Canadian history, the communist-run Canadian seamen's union has been flooding Halifax and other Canadian ports with misleading advertisements and handbills concerning the sale of Canadian ships and hiring of aliens to man ships purchased or chartered by foreign interests.
The story then lists a number of facts with which I need not burden the house, and then goes on to comment:
Ostensibly the CSU has tried to improve working conditions and wages for Canadian seamen, but the end result of CSU policy has been that, while the jobs are better, Canadian ships are being hounded out of business and the jobs go with them.
CSU supporters are spreading propaganda to the effect that wages make up only ten per cent or thereabouts of the operating expenses of Canadian ships, when thirty-three per cent would be nearer the truth. Moreover, union tactics prevent Canadian seamen from doing efficient work in shipshape fashion, thus forcing ships' maintenance cost to record heights.
The story then refers to the handbills mentioned earlier.
On Tuesday of this week landlubber members of the CSU distributed on the streets of Halifax a handbill allegedly printed in Montreal, which was entitled "Canadian seamen become D.P.'s!"
The advertisement stated that:
"This is what idle seamen and idle ships mean to Nova Scotia.
"It means more lay-offs for shipyard workers.
"It means jobless seamen.
"It means empty shipyards.
"It means less work for freight handlers, longshoremen and other waterfront workers.
"Halifax's prosperity depends upon a busy waterfront !
"Save Canada's merchant marine! Maintain employment in the maritimes."
This is all true, Mr. Speaker; there is danger of Canadian ships being driven from the seas. But the real argument is as to who is responsible for this unpleasant possibility and what can be done to remedy the situation. I would ask the hon. member for Cape Breton South and others who adopt his argument to have some consideration for those experienced Canadian seamen who have no sympathy with the radical views and destructive intentions of the leaders of the Canadian seamen's union. Men who have followed the sea for years find themselves unable to secure employment in their calling because of their fundamental disagreement with the union bosses. Their places have been taken by younger and less experienced men whose qualification is simply that they

are more inclined to listen to and agree with the radical views of those union leaders.
I would ask the hon. gentleman also to have some consideration for the men who, with great effort and ability, have built up the Canadian merchant marine. Often in this house the hon. member has pointed out that the profit motive is of importance to business men. I think he would be the first to admit from his experience that as long as the owners of a business find they can profitably keep it in operation, they will make every effort to do so and continue to make their profits. I know he will also have to admit that in the socialist state he advocates activities of a commercial nature will be carried on by the state with a close approximation of this attention to profitable operation. Recent experience in Saskatchewan has indicated that a socialist government will not hesitate to close down commercial operations which under existing circumstances it cannot see its way clear to continue. In view of this, does the hon. member expect this house or the country to believe that Canadian shipowners are intentionally destroying their own business, the Canadian merchant marine, while it is still possible to operate it under existing conditions?
The fact is that under existing conditions, brought about largely by the Canadian seamen's union, the operators of the Canadian merchant marine find that under present high costs they cannot continue to operate in competition with ships of other flags. If the Canadian merchant marine is to be saved- and it is of supreme importance, Mr. Speaker, that it be saved-it will be necessary for the shipowners and seamen to come to agreements which will permit Canadian ships to operate on a competitive basis with those sailing under the flags of other maritime nations.
There is one matter of some considerable national interest and significance to which I should like to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, and that of the house. On June 21 of this year the city of Halifax will celebrate the two hundredth anniversary of its founding in the year 1749. Halifax is the oldest English speaking settlement in that great portion of North America which is ndw the Dominion of Canada. An anniversary of this nature is a milestone in the life not only of the city itself but of the province of Nova Scotia and of the country as a whole. Patriotism and proper national pride find their firm and enduring basis in a long and proud history. We in this country have the advantage of enjoying an almost unique mingling of two main currents of history and culture. The city of Halifax and the city of Quebec share the leading roles in
The Address-Mr. Dickey these two histories. Throughout colonial times, these two cities, by reason of their early establishment and strategic situations, were the focal points about which the events of history revolved.
The story of Halifax's two hundred years as an organized community is preceded by a history of the use of its magnificent harbour as a haven for mariners and fishermen which goes back to the days of the earliest Norse voyagers. The whole of this history will be commemorated by the celebrations which will mark the observance of this bicentennial, and which will continue over a period of some two months. Halifax has been preparing energetically for many months to make suitable arrangements for appropriate commemoration of this event. Halifax hopes to welcome many visitors from all over this continent and elsewhere in this her bicentennial year. The best possible provisions are being made for the entertainment and accommodation of everyone who may find it possible to accept our most cordial invitation to attend our birthday party. I hope that many members of this house will do us the honour of paying us a visit.
Mr. Speaker, I have left to the end one extremely pleasant task, and that is to congratulate the three new ministers of the crown who joined the government during the recess. The selection of all three of these gentlemen to the honourable posts to which they have been called has been greeted with the most profound satisfaction. I shall perhaps be forgiven if I single out the new minister from Nova Scotia for a special word of congratulation and good wishes. The Hon. R. H. Winters follows hard on the heels of a minister of the crown of many years' experience, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, who was a great Nova Scotian and a great Canadian. Looking into the more distant past, he follows a most illustrious line of ministers of the crown from Nova Scotia. In his exacting task I can say to the new minister that his colleagues in this house, and all those who know him, look to him with confidence to maintain the great tradition of those who have gone before him.

I know that "fair" means two things. It means not good and not enough. He is not going to admit that. I should like to read what the Calgary Albertan had to say about the statements made at this convention. They refer to the fact that Mr. Prowse must be a politician and can be expected to take the politician's viewpoint:
But still it was a shock to hear him make two particular points in an address to the recent Liberal convention in Calgary. One point was that the voters should side with the party they think is going to win, so they will have a "friend at court." The other was that Alberta, with only two Liberal M.P.'s at Ottawa, got a fair share of federal money, and could be expected to do much better by increasing its Liberal representation.
And then again:
But we would like to think that federal governments would distribute available moneys among the provinces with regard only to need and other such considerations, and without regard to how those provinces voted. We would like to think that voters would vote for what they thought was the best party, not the one with the best chance of winning. We would appreciate the federal Liberal party appealing to the Alberta electorate on its record and on issues and not on "having a friend at court" and getting government grants.
The next paragraph is significant:
Come to think of it, Alberta has been "agin" the federal government for going on to twenty-eight years. In all that time the contingent of Alberta M.P.'s has been in the opposition at Ottawa. Yet Alberta seems to be doing fairly well. Perhaps Mr. Prowse doesn't understand the people of this province.
That goes for my hon. friends opposite too. We have before us an amendment to the amendment to which I wish to refer just

briefly. The first part of the amendment to the amendment calls for the orderly marketing of our natural products, and for their exchange for goods needed in Canada, and for the elimination of speculation in foodstuffs. We have no argument with that. Then they say:
We regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provision for national health insurance.
In connection with that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that our conception of national health insurance is likely to be quite a different one from the conception of national health insurance held by my hon. friends of the C.C.F. In order that there may be no misunderstanding whatsoever I should like to make abundantly clear what kind of insurance we shall be voting for when we vote for the amendment to the amendment.
We have always taken the position that the health of every individual should be looked upon as one of our greatest natural resources. The healthy individual is able to make the greatest contribution to production, and to the arts and sciences. The physical well-being of every individual must, therefore, be recognized as of major concern and responsibility to the nation. During the war that concern and that responsibility were acknowledged by Canada. Our servicemen were provided with nourishing food, suitable environment and effective physical training, as well as with necessary dental, medical, optical and hospital services free of charge.

By the Canadian taxpayers. All the money came out of taxes imposed on the people of Canada. We claim that a national health policy is absolutely necessary, and it should include all health measures, and all citizens should have access to them regardless of means.
Poverty, leading to malnutrition, unsanitary slum conditions, drudgery and mental anxiety, are direct causes of physical and mental degeneration. Economic insecurity of those who live just above the poverty line encourages a false economy. Through fear, such people starve themselves or resort to cheap remedies in place of proper health services.
Because of a rising demand on the part of the people of Canada for health services available to all, suggestions of compulsory and contributory state health insurance schemes have come from various quarters. This involves compulsion, and regimentation of doctors, nurses and patients, and the people, with higher direct taxation upon all. Such a policy is, in our opinion, undemocratic and unsound economically. Social Crediters are

convinced that a national health policy must involve six things. They are:
1.	Steps toward abolition of poverty through the adoption of sound economic policies which assure a basic income to provide economic security in unemployment, sickness, disability or old age, and opportunity for a decent standard of living.
2.	Progress towards non-contributory national health services available to all citizens irrespective of means, without regimentation of patients, doctors or hospital authorities.
3.	Adequate grants-in-aid for the construction and maintenance of hospitals for curative services, and for all measures of sickness prevention, including research.
4.	Encouragement of voluntary mutual schemes of sickness insurance, supplementary to national health services, for occupational groups, communities and others.
5.	The systematic introduction of the principle of payment for keeping people in good health instead of placing the medical profession in the unenviable position of benefiting only in proportion to the ill health of the nation.
6.	Physical culture to be promoted as an essential aspect of the national life.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to reassert what I said earlier. We are ready to support the amendment to the amendment, but laying particular emphasis upon the statement I made that the type of national health insurance for which we shall vote is the type of national health insurance which I have just put on the record.

Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne affords private members of the House of Commons an opportunity to discuss a redress of grievances. There are a great many grievances in this country today. I may say that one of them comes from the main tax-paying city of the dominion, Toronto. We have not had a representative in the cabinet since 1935 whereas we used to have four or five at one time from that large centre of industry, finance and education. In my opinion that is a mistake. I have no doubt there will be a change very shortly.
The old parties are just like old soldiers. They never die. They may be recreated, and all that kind of thing. I hope the day is not far distant when the party on this side of the house may be recreated because I am one of those who believe in a national government. I am in favour of a national government for our party in every province of the dominion. In two of the provinces they have what they
The Address-Mr. Church call a union government. One of them is in British Columbia. However, it may be that the coast will face invasion very shortly.
I am going to refer to the battle of the Pacific in a few minutes. I believe we would be far better off if we had a national Conservative government there. Then we could get something done regarding national affairs because, as I see it, in the Pacific coast province the only alternative is to vote for what you might call a quasi-government on the other side of the fence.
When the late Mr. Wendell Willkie was told after the 1940 presidential election that his views were contrary to his campaign speeches he ridiculed the idea and called it an insult because he said his former statements were only campaign oratory. I notice that President Truman is not slow to follow that example. According to what I read in the papers, and in the records of congress, since his election he has followed the example of Mr. Wendell Willkie regarding the Taft-Hartley Act, wage increases, and relations between labour and management generally. His words now are contrary to his campaign speeches. At the present time in all these involved matters he just wants to act the part of an umpire instead of taking sides. Therefore I say to members of the government, and all those on the other side of the house, that they may see the mote in our eye but they do not see the beam in their own eye.
One of the matters on which I wish to say something refers to the reform of the Senate. I should like some of the frontbenchers to listen to what I am going to say. I should like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), and all the rest of them, to listen. I should like my friends the members for York West and York South to come back here because I am going to have something to say to the Minister of Transport. As I say, I should like to have the attention of the member for York South. I think it would be far better if he would leave the Minister of Transport and come over here, because I am going to refer to the lack of steam suburban service for the Toronto district which affects his riding.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I shall be glad to listen.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I like the members of the
cabinet personally, but I say to this government that they may see the mote in the eye of those over here, but they cannot see the beam in their own eye. Talk about reform of the Senate, which has been referred to by my hon. friends to the left. On many occasions I was told in this house by the former Prime Minister that he would have a conference with the members of the other place to

The Address-Mr. Church see if they could not be given more work. Why, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for even a Victoria Cross holder to occupy a bench over in that other place. Some here spoke of moving the Senate over to Hull. 1 was not here that night. Then they spoke of moving them to the east block; and finally it was suggested in the house that they be moved to the printing bureau, which, it was said, would be a splendid place, since they would be in no danger there, with so many fire escapes on the building.
I believe the time has come when we should have some consideration for the province of Ontario. I am not one of those who try to get rich by being a member of parliament. Far from it. I think if I had stayed home altogether I would have been far better off. One of the things Canada should have learned from recent events is the tremendous popularity of the British royal family in this country. Another thing we must have noticed is the tremendous decline of the House of Commons as a result of surrendering its powers to the executive. Why that should be I do not know, but it is a fact, and unless there is a change in some of the newspapers, the radio and so on, so the people back home in our constituencies may know what is going on, we might just as well be meeting at times in secret, for all the people know of what is going on here.
The Canadian people rejoice in being subjects of His Majesty the King. As Canadians we are citizens of a free association of nations. The events last fall in Britain, including the illness of the king and the birth of a prince, made more apparent than ever the feelings of the Canadian people. And when Their Majesties visited Canada in 1939, nowhere did they get a better reception than in the province of Quebec. On her return to England the queen is reported to have said that the trip across Canada was something like a second coronation; and that was certainly due them for the good work they had performed.
I am more of a sportsman than a politician, and I want to congratulate one great citizen, Sir Donald Bradman, who was knighted by the king for his services to sport in general and to cricket in particular. I believe it was last New Year's day that a well deserved tribute was paid to that great Australian who has done so much for this old sport. Last June, July and August, when some members of this house were in England, they had an opportunity to see the Australian team defeat England. I have known him for a long time; he came to our city a few times, and I had a letter from him. He has become a household 
word, so much so that a prominent member of the British house, a Labour member who admires him, in speaking of the controls in force in that country, said an umpire might just as well try to show Bradman how to hold his bat as for the government to attempt some of the things it has been carrying on.
I was very glad to see that at its last convention my party advocated some measures of relief for the municipalities throughout Canada. One recommendation was that federal crown properties should pay some form of municipal tax for local services, such as fire and police protection and all the other things for which the city of Ottawa is paid half a million dollars. The provinces pay local taxes on their property, and it seems to me this government should do the same. I do not want our party to be called by any fancy prefixes or affixes. I am a Conservative first, last and all the time. I have no objection if the party wishes to add the word "Progressive" but I am too modest to call myself progressive, though I have brought before the house yearly many progressive measures. One of these was the national fuel policy, which I fathered in 1922. Another was parliamentary, constitutional, cabinet and law reform, one of the most important problems yet unsolved. Another was national flood control and irrigation, while another was oil pipe lines and petroleum development. I remember years ago when we had the floods in the Don river. The bridge collapsed and in later years we had to divert the Don. I also called attention to our three main problems of empire trade, defence and migration, and urged a cut of fifty per cent in all civilian estimates.
Today we have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent by outside boards and bodies without the authorization of this House of Commons. We never hear of the millions of dollars these people are spending over our heads, until we find it all charged up to the government. There is an old German proverb which says that saving is a greater art than spending. Saving is the essence of progress. We have an old proverb of our own, look after the pence and the pounds will look after themselves. That is still true; look after the cents and the dollars will look after themselves. Thrift is a great virtue. Who said that? Cicero. We should revive the old sense of personal responsibility in public affairs and see to it that the government does not squander our savings. We must never forget the old principle, that money must not be spent without representation, the disregard of which caused all the trouble in America which culminated in the Boston tea party. I

The Address-Mr. Church
referred to this point in the house last year, in regard to the winding up of the penny bank, which taught school children the importance of thrift.
I was very glad to see the suggestion that there should be an immediate restoration of the empire air training plan, especially in view of the statement made recently by Air Marshal Tedder in regard to Britain's position in the event of trouble. Then I believe there should be a housecleaning in the C.B.C., which has been a most mischievous institution. Nobody should have free time; everybody should pay. There are hundreds and hundreds of these employees, and some of them never had jobs before. Yet we in this House of Commons cannot find out anything about the salaries that are paid. Everyone knows the salaries paid in the House of Commons; everyone knows how much the judges are paid; yet these people are brought to Toronto from all over Canada to work for this corporation. Then think of the cheap and ridiculous nonsense that we hear from the C.B.C. board of governors. If I had my way I would dismiss the whole lot of them, with the exception of the member from Toronto, Fred Crawford, who is a very good man.
Reference has been made also to provincial rights. Look at the Sirois report, one of the most mischievous documents ever compiled. If we are to have unity in Canada we must have unity between Ontario and Quebec, the keystone provinces of confederation. Although before the second war those two provinces paid about 70 per cent of all the cash taxes, they received little or nothing in the way of expenditures. I am for provincial and municipal rights, first, last and all the time. I would apply the old Conservative doctrine, each for all and all for each, as a principle of confederation for the provinces. I believe in bonuses, subventions and subsidies, as a federal remedy to aid in part in solving all provincial wrongs. I am opposed to any more political railway rate structures, and to fastening them on the two central provinces. Ontario was the forgotten province so far as the Canadian National Railways were concerned.
For many years past I have been asking for steam suburban service like that which Montreal and every American city has. I have here in my hand timetables of the Canadian National Railways and of the Canadian Pacific Railway for the city of Montreal. In Toronto we have one train a day out to Lome Park. If we had some support we might get something better. When I was head of the city I raised this matter, but it has not been taken up since. I introduced a bill here. We compelled the old Grand Trunk railway, which was swallowed up by the Canadian National railway, to issue commutation tickets; because it was in Ontario that the old Grand Trunk railway made all its money. I would ask hon. members to look at the service in western Ontario and in the Niagara district. I succeeded in getting commutation tickets for Oakville, Brampton and some other places. Here is a list of trains of the Canadian National Railways in the Montreal district. If some newspaper would publish them, it might do some good. I am surprised that the Toronto press do nothing about this matter. If my suggestion were followed it would relieve the whole housing situation in the Toronto district. That would follow if we had in the Toronto district the same suburban service which Montreal has-trains every fifteen minutes out to Dixie, Lakeside and all those places, as they have to Lachine, Dorval and so on. The national railways should not have had its head offices in Montreal, but in the public-ownership city of Toronto. It was in Ontario that the old Grand Trunk made their money. What did they do? The province of Ontario suffered. It was then made the C.N.R. under Sir Henry Thornton, and they spent money like water. They would have given an air service to the sun, the moon and the stars if they had only been allowed to spend the money. What it simply amounted to was that Ontario got nothing. The result is that on both railways the situation is the same. I am really surprised, because there is nothing which would have increased housing, health and other services uiuic iu a ciiy of our size and done more for the benefit of the rising generation. We do not ask for anything just for fun. We ask that we get similar treatment, and we are not getting it from that railway at the present time.
I complained about the C.N.R. service in the Toronto district, and referred to the Canadian National railways disaster in my constituency at Riverdale and Degrassi street last June. At that time a freight train jumped the track and cattle wandered all over the district. I urged the railways to lessen the speed of trains on the viaduct. A similar accident happened a month or so afterwards at the King street subway. If a streetcar had been going past at the time, the train would have jumped over on the streetcar. Another accident of the same kind happened at the Parkdale station. There should be a new C.N.R. station at Sunnyside and north Parkdale, two of the most used stations in Canada. The accommodation at the two Parkdale stations and at the Union station for women and children and for the comfort of passengers and trainmen is a relic of the

The Address-Mr. Church past and is becoming a nuisance as compared with rest room accommodation in Montreal, Hamilton and London. I may say that I am glad to see them get something, but it was in Ontario that the Canadian National Railways made most of its money.
Since I entered the House of Commons I have had the unanimous support of labour. In the past I have had a great deal to do with labour and have settled many strikes. When the streetcar strike took place on the old Toronto street railway, I met a great man, Mr. Gompers, president of the American federation of labour, Mr. Mahone and Mr. Fitzgerald. Together we sat down and with others settled that strike.
I may say that in conjunction with my late beloved friend, Mr. Woodsworth, when I first came to parliament I introduced a motion in favour of unemployment insurance and old age pensions. I happened to be the president of the union of Canadian municipalities when we were urging this thing in the early 1920's and before. We had hundreds of employees in the various departments in the city of Toronto, with a payroll running into millions of dollars. Some of them went to the first war and afterwards returned to their old positions in the city's service. Then we had the school board, public utilities, the harbour board, and hydro, and later on, the transportation commission, all with a large number of employees and a big payroll.
Before the present government introduced the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940, some of the municipalities in Ontario went to Queen's Park, Mr. Hepburn then being premier, and we were told that under the Municipal Act we could not legally pay our employees on retirement $12 a week, as we used to on pension for many years. It was little enough, goodness knows, but we were told we had no power to do it and that it was quite wrong. I do not want to impose any undue burden on the employer; far from it. Unemployment insurance has been a splendid thing for the country. There were certain defects in the law and they were cured last session. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) did good work on it, and the municipalities suggested some changes in the act, which he made.
Never has the House of Commons been faced with graver issues than now. At the present time we face the most serious economic disaster and a very direct military threat, as we go on pretending we have security. We also err, as does the United States, in taking Britain's supremacy of the seas for granted. There is only one path to take, and our Ottawa government will not follow it, namely, empire consolidation, which stood us so well in two long wars.


Why is any scheme of internationalism, however absurd, adopted by Ottawa instead of finding real security within our own family members in the dominions and crown colonies? The United Nations is heading us into a third war, and the west as yet is now no match for the east. Canada will soon learn the sham of depending on Washington's aid alone, without the aid of Britain and the empire, which protected us for four centuries.
Stalin's Russia is as dangerous to the peace of the world as was Hitler's Germany; and Russia, by waging a weaponless war, has already conquered huge areas of Europe and Asia. I find an analogy between the failure of the United States and Britain to occupy Berlin, and the failure of Hannibal to enter ancient Rome when only fifteen miles away. The next year Carthage was destroyed.
I note that 38,000 tons of rubber are being exported monthly from Malaya to Russia, while Canada and the empire get little or none. If the government is sincere, it should have sought defence and security, as we did safely and well in two long wars, jointly within our own family along with the dominions and crown colonies, when together with the mother country we had to go it alone for two and a half years. During the time that Russia was an ally of Germany the United States did not come in, in a military way, for over two years until the time of Pearl Harbor. I here and now ask the government in this debate-and I think I have a right to demand it of the government and its servants-that proper means be taken to see that our armed forces are prepared with effective plans for our defence, including home defence services, and that they be put on a war footing in case of an emergency. I refer to the home guard and all that kind of thing.
Now we should provide for our own defence. Without the aid of the dominions and the empire we have no defence. All our defences are based on the fact that in two long wars Britain had the supremacy of the seas. That was the real Monroe doctrine. That saved America and the world in two long wars. Now we shall have to see to our own defence, since Britain cannot do it, and it is going to cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
What is the issue in Berlin? As I told the house last June, the issue in Berlin is the command of the seas. The government claim that they never had an invitation. The United States did not need an invitation. Britain does not need an invitation and Australia does not need an invitation. The chief Air Marshal of Britain said that we are in great danger today. Britain is in grave danger today of an air raid in case of war.

Russia would be over Britain in a few minutes. Here we are asleep. The government are asleep. They do not realize the issue. The real issue in Berlin today is the command of the seas. If Britain is driven out, if America is driven out of there, then we are going to lose command of the seas. To whom? To Russia. I fail to see why Canada is not ready after all the urgings we have had. It looks to me now as if we are back to the days of Ethelred who was called Ethelred the Unready many long years ago. That is what Canada's defences are, unready. We have lost Britain; now, to defend ourselves, we have to make a deal with whom? With Washington. I remember when some of our friends in the house said in the first war and in the second war, "Why do we need to go to London for defence, when we can get all the defence we need in Washington"? Yet what happened? Two and a half years passed before they came in, in both wars. It was not until after Pearl Harbor that they came in in the last war. If that is all the defence we have, I fear we are going to be invaded. There is all this talk about nationalism and defence forces. A million men from the dominions went over in the first war under their own status, sovereignty and autonomy. One hundred and thirty-five thousand of these men fell in battle. They went over voluntarily. They did not go to fight for Britain. They went over to fight by her side, and what they did changed the whole history of the world. In the second war they went over in numbers ten times larger, with their own status, autonomy and sovereignty, and of their volition.
Today we talk about regional pacts. Well, there were regional pacts a hundred years ago. You know, regional pacts are just scraps of paper. In four centuries Britain had command of the seas and saved America's shores against Philip of Spain, Louis XIV and Napoleon, and twice in our generation the mother country has saved the world from slavery. Yet today there are those who ridicule her. We would have had the awful horrors of war on our own soil but for her. Last year I saw the cove where the enemy came. They came up the St. Laurence river as far as Riviere du Loup. We had to call a private meeting of the House of Commons to talk about the navy. I can say to my hon. friends from Quebec that they would have experienced the horrors of war on their own soil if the enemy had ever landed there, and hundreds of thousands of our people would have been killed or carted away. The tramping of feet would have been heard not only in the maritimes but in Ontario and Quebec and tens of thousands of people would
The Address-Mr. Church have been carted away to work in the mines of Germany and Europe. We should not forget those who saved our soil in two long wars. I believe that the day is not far distant when something will have to be done about it.
I may say that for the first time in forty years Britain faces every possible threat of a war without a military ally of any consequence or strength and the whole continent of Europe will soon be dominated by Russia. In the first world war she had a very great friend who was then one of the most formidable of military powers, France. In the second world war France again was our friend and ally, although weaker, and after nine months she withered away. France is not what she used to be but she is friendly. In a military way she is somewhat powerless. Her economic affairs have improved somewhat. The net result is that Canada takes no part in the real issue.
The western union powers so far are more imaginary than real, and the Atlantic pact is somewhat up in the clouds and fog, although I hope it will be a success. Britain cannot join any customs union in Europe. If the western union means, co-operation with European countries that have not our way of life, and are alien to Anglo-American ideas of liberty and civilization, it is time for us to clear away the Atlantic pact fog of the present time.
I notice the criticism in the Economist and other papers that the Atlantic pact will be useless without any military forces to back it up. The United States could have entered Prague, instead of halting their forces at Pilsen. That created the present Berlin situation, and possibly also this Carthaginian peace. It is time that something should be done about it.
Amidst all this, it is too bad that British leadership is not more agressive. I venture to say that if Mr. Churchill and Mr. Eden were leading the government over in that country they would long ago have met Stalin and candidly discussed with him the whole world situation and would have told him that the west meant business from the start. They would have persuaded him to change his tactics because he needs capital goods from all these western places. We already know the weaknesses of the military strength of the Brussels powers, backed by the United States and the British empire. We should avoid placing arms in the hands of the German people, who might abuse them again. The Russian satellites are torn between fear of Russia and fear of Germany, and the western powers will bring on a third war if they persist in rearming Germany. It will divide the west also. The duty of the west now is

The Address-Mr. Church to oi'ganize its military strength and to make Russia and her satellites believe that the disunity and indecision of the west are over once and for all. The west is as yet no match for the east, but if a start is made it will be better, and there is no use depending on any security from Lake Success, and such appeasement methods, which were a distinct failure in two world wars, instead of depending on our own strength from within the empire.
From the town of Yalta western statesmen have gone out of their way to demonstrate friendliness to Russia. Britain withdrew her armies, and the Americans halted at Pilsen. The result of this awful folly is now seen in the very critical situation in Berlin. Within a very few days of Japan's surrender Russia was actually invited by the Americans to declare war on Japan in order that she might participate in occupation of the Japanese empire conquered by British and American armies, and taking full advantage she at once seized and flooded Manchuria, seized the armament factories at Mukden and handed them over to the Chinese communists who have thereby been assisted in their war against the Chinese government.
The position is so serious that, unless the western allies help, it may be too late. They have provided equipment to Russia, to the point where the Chinese are likely to become communist, and will be dominated by Russia. In view of this, we should put all proper safeguards in the Atlantic pact which we will have before us shortly. Today from the Baltic to the Aegean, from the Danube to the Yellow sea, Moscow has produced a dismal picture. Each time we adopt appeasement and offer a helping hand, each time we offer appeasement to Russia, we do it at the expense of our friends, and it is interpreted by Stalin as a sign of weakness. As a consequence seven countries in Europe, together with China, have been enslaved. Other countries in Asia and throughout the world are threatened. These are the facts.
But no one is ready to do anything about it, What is the use of pretending that we have security, as we do pretend, when in fact we have not got it?
Then, I should like to refer to the Pacific, because in the Pacific ocean we used to have our protection from the United States. At the time of the first war Japan looked after the Pacific, with the result that the United States and Great Britain were able to devote their energies to the other theatre of war. However, as I pointed out in the house before the beginning of the second world war, at the time of that war the situation was quite different. We had a long coast line stretch-

ing 760 miles from Puget Sound to Queen Charlotte islands. That coast line is absolutely unprotected. What are we going to do about it, so far as Russia is concerned? She has a powerful fleet and air force at the present time. And, I can tell you this, that she may be out there quicker than you think.
The Pacific question should be an empire question. Australia is interested in the Pacific. It was shown during the air debate three or four years ago, and it has been shown in Australia and in Canada, that we have a vast interest in the Pacific. Our position there should be studied; and I hope the government will study it before another session of parliament is called.
But Canada has a regular expeditionary force on all the seven seas. We have our people - thirty ambassadors - travelling all over the world. I think the Auditor General ought to get busy on this matter, and we would have some relief; because each one of them has a first secretary, a second secretary and a third secretary. I am sure I do not know what he does; perhaps he carries a jug of ice water, or something like that.
We do know however that we have all those embassies, a fact which was ridiculed last June by the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot). At that time he was referring to so many of these ambassadors, and pointed out that if he were on Sparks street he would want to take the middle of the road. They all want to be at the head of the band. And we might bear in mind that the undertaker is the first man in the procession, too. These ambassadors are like drum majors who throw their drumsticks in the air and are very impressive.
All this is a mistake, this sending of amateur diplomats who learn from experience. Because that is all they are, every one of them. Some secretaries have to go along with the ministers, of course. They are always followed by their secretaries. I am not criticizing anyone's having a trip; I am always glad to see a person take a trip-but not when he is spending the country's money.
I notice my good friend the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. McCubbin) is not here this evening. I may say however that last fall I was in his constituency attending the funeral of an archbishop. I never saw such glorious country in my life as one sees in the county of Middlesex. But I can tell you this, that up there I saw no churches blown down, the way they were blown down in the old country. We read that the Right Reverend Bishop Renison had to celebrate communion in the ruins of Coventry cathedral, and hold the ceremony in the open air.

I do not wish to refer to my good friend the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture. I would not object to his taking a trip. But the Auditor General should look into this expeditionary force of ours. Why, they would reach four deep from here to Lansdowne park. I notice the ministers of Health and Labour are not in their seats; but I believe they have forty or fifty fellows out on the high seas now, on their way to study hygiene, and all that sort of thing. Is it any wonder that the people are confused?
There should be a 75 per cent reduction in our expenditures. We used to run this country, at the time Sir Wilfrid Laurier came in, and Sir Charles Tupper went out, for about $36 million. But today we are away up around $4 billion. It is away up in the air-up in the clouds. I say when the figures become astronomical like that the money is being blown in such a way that nothing is gained. So I do hope something will be done about it.
At this session of parliament we as a House of Commons must concern ourselves with matters touching the very lives of our people. It is a first duty of a government to look after the peace, welfare, health, happiness and prosperity of its citizens. These are the primary considerations. We meet here surrounded by a cloud of witnesses from the constituencies, the people back home who are suffering today in this battle of life, the people who are struggling to make a living.
We should deal with the lives of the masses of the people, and the matters which concern them. We should deal with food and poor housing. This evening I said that we should have steam suburban transportation. I pointed out that taxation was too high, and that we should have national health insurance. The average elector is in need of some help in these ways.
I was in hopes that we might have some amendment to our Unemployment Insurance Act. Our labouring people could get some help in this way. Then, there should be some food subsidy, along the lines I have suggested. I hope something will be done about that too, for the low bracket wage earners.
At the present time the only sure salvation for peace, and the prevention of war, rests upon the strength of our allies. As Mr. Churchill has said, the only sure foundation for peace and the prevention of actual war rests upon strength. We owe a duty to our empire to stay strong in peace. We can be friendly only with co-operative neighbours.
