speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), when speaking in this debate, moved the following amendment:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provision for the orderly marketing of our natural products, and for their exchange for goods needed in Canada, and for the elimination of speculation in foodstuffs; We regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provision for national health insurance.
I rise to endorse wholeheartedly that amendment to the amendment. I do so because, first, I am a firm believer in national marketing legislation and the necessity for the establishment in this country of a national marketing agency to market our primary products. I support this amendment also because I am aware of the fact that the organized farmers of this country have for some years been pressing this government to pass such legislation. I may say further that the birthplace of this type of legislation was the southern interior of British Columbia. I remember when the first committee sat to make a draft bill for the provincial legislature and I am happy to know that the draft bill presented to the cabinet by the Canadian federation of agriculture was originally drafted by the officials and delegates of the British Columbia fruit growers association. You will realize, therefore, that this legislation is of great interest to the people I have the honour to represent and to the people of Yale constituency.
I could speak at greater length on this subject but I have already spoken briefly on the matter this session. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) dealt very fully and effectively with this matter when speaking in this debate. I know the serious position facing the tree fruit industry in British Columbia and other agricultural producers as a result of this government not listening to the argument put forward by the producers. I am speaking as one who believes that if we are going to retain or recapture the United Kingdom and European markets

The Address-Mr. Herridge we cannot in the future permit the question of dollars to interfere with the exchange of our commodities.
I also support this amendment because I believe the Canadian people are looking forward to the establishment of a national health insurance scheme. I admit that the present grants in aid are a step in the right direction and will bring about some improvement in hospital and other services, but I am sure, and I believe many hon. members of this house are sure, that we will not have a worthwhile health insurance scheme until the national and provincial governments work together in co-operation with the people of Canada.
, I am quite sure that the veterans of this country and their dependents are disappointed that there is no mention of veterans affairs in the speech from the throne. I am sure that those veterans who are at pic^ut living cn the -..*oc-.nt p ,)f war veterans allowances are disappointed. I am sure the veterans organizations in this country are disappointed. I am sure the veterans who only had the opportunity to serve in England in the first war are disappointed. I am certain the imperial veterans who have resided in Canada for a long period of years are disappointed.
In addition, I am quite sure the old age pensioners of this country, who are living under increasingly difficult conditions from month to month, are disappointed, having knowledge of the large financial surplus which this government will quite likely announce, that some further remedy has not been proposed for their most unfortunate condition. I could deal at length with controls, subsidies, housing and other matters, but I am going to be brief on a few matters tonight.
I wish to take the opportunity this evening to deal with a matter of great importance to the people of the southern interior of British Columbia, a matter that they are greatly concerned about. Having criticized the speech briefly, I am pleased to note that the government will introduce an amendment to the Supreme Court Act to make the Supreme Court of Canada the court of last resort. This is something that has been advocated by this group for some years, most effectively to my personal knowledge during recent sessions of parliament by the hon. member for Kinders-ley (Mr. Jaenicke). I think that is a step forward in legislation in this country.
I am glad the government has indicated that it intends to introduce a bill to broaden the scope of family allowances. It sounds as though it will be all to the good and make family allowances available to a larger number of deserving people. I am also pleased 
to see in the address that a measure is to be introduced to provide assistance to the provinces in building a trans-Canada highway system. This announcement will be of great interest to the people of British Columbia, and to the people of the southern interior of British Columbia particularly. This is all I am going to say at this time because I hope to have something more to say on this matter at a later date.
I notice that the government has proposals for the development of navigation and power on the great lakes and in the St. Lawrence basin. I heartily support the proposals for the development of the St. Lawrence basin, but I want to take advantage of this opportunity to bring to the attention of the house the importance of the development of another great river basin in this country, of which some hon. members are unaware and of which the majority of people in Eastern Canada are totally unaware. I refer to the Canadian portion of the Columbia river basin.
The people of the Okanagan and the people of Kootenay are vitally concerned with the possible development of this vast basin. They are concerned with it because it means power for irrigation, it means power for secondary industries, it means power for agriculture, and it means power for the establishment of a large pulp industry in Kootenay West, the district which I represent.
Before proceeding to deal briefly with a review of the resources of the basin, I should like to describe the basin, and I will give the official description, which is as follows:
The Columbia river basin is situated in the cordillera on the Pacific slope of the North American continent where its river system comprises one of the large international drainages shared by Canada and the United States. It includes approximately 259,000 square miles, between north latitudes 41 and 53 degrees and west longitudes 110 and 124 degrees. Of this vast area, some 39,700 square miles form the southeast portion of the province of British Columbia in Canada, while the 219,300 square miles in the United States include almost all of Idaho, the greater part of Oregon and Washington, western Montana and relatively small areas of western Wyoming, northwestern Utah and northeastern Nevada. The greatest width of the basin, from western Wyoming to the Pacific ocean, is 728 miles, and its maximum length, from its most northerly limit in British Columbia, to its southern boundary in northern Nevada, is 818 miles.
This vast area is capable of great development. The Canadian section of this huge triangle, about which I am going to speak briefly this evening, can be best described as starting from the junction of the Alberta and British Columbia boundaries with the international boundary, proceeding northwest along the ridge of the Rocky mountain slope to the watershed of the Canoe river which flows into the big bend of the Columbia. Then it turns southwest and follows the height of

land between the Columbia divide and the Thompson divide for possibly some thirty miles on the west side of the Arrow lakes, and then, roughly speaking, proceeds southwest towards the international boundary at a point south of Princeton.
There are four great tributaries of the Columbia river which are of major concern to Canadians. They are the Okanagan, the Kootenay, the Pend-d'Oreille and the Kettle. The international character of the basin is exemplified by the course of the Columbia, Kootenay and Pend-d'Oreille rivers, and is further demonstrated by the Flat Head, Okanagan, Similkameen and numerous smaller streams which cross the international border once or more on their way to the Columbia and its tributaries.
In order to bring to the attention of the house the great resources of the basin I will review them very briefly. I may say that my figures are based on federal government reports, provincial government reports, and reports issued by various organizations and commissions. They are only approximate, but they are approximately correct. The Canadian portion of the Columbia river basin has a population of approximately 125,000 people. Of that 125,000 people approximately 42,000 are urban dwellers and 83,000 are rural or country dwellers. The power resources of the Columbia river basin in Canada amount to about 450,000 kilowatts installed at the present time. The major portion of this is the result of the developments of the West Kootenay Power and Light Company, and the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company on the lower portion of the Kootenay river where they have an installed capacity at the present time of 258,000 kilowatts. The difference between the 258,000 and 450,000 kilowatts is found in some installations on the Elk river, and on various smaller streams throughout the basin. The estimated total that can be developed on the main stem of the Columbia beyond the big bend at Revelstoke and to the international boundary is 2,900,000 kilowatts. This amount can be developed with control and regulation. The estimated potential development of electrical energy in the whole of the Canadian portion of the Columbia river basin is about 4,000,000 kilowatts. Therefore you can see the great possibilities for the development of power, and the opportunity to apply that power to vast and undeveloped natural resources.
At the present time the agricultural resources of the basin are extensive, although they are capable of immense development. There is a total of 305,400 acres under cultivation. Of that number 75,500 acres are
The Address-Mr. Herridge irrigated. An additional 395,000 acres are in use as open grazing land. The value of the 8,000 farms in the basin, with the land, buildings and improvements, is over $60 million. The present annual production of fruit, dairy products, grain, livestock, poultry, seeds, hay, honey, and other farm produce, is about $35 million. There are still many thousands of acres to be irrigated, many thousands of acres to be cleared, and many thousands of acres to be drained.
Turning to forest resources, 13 per cent of the productive forest land in British Columbia is in the Canadian portion of the Columbia river basin.1 It is estimated there are 22 billion board feet of timber within the basin, of which amount 14 billion board feet are classified as accessible. That amount is being increased from year to year with the development of bigger logging equipment, and cheaper methods of building roads and developing communications. For some years the annual lumber cut has been over 300 million board feet per year. In addition to that there is an enormous quantity of cedar poles, piling, ties, mine timber, mine props, shingle bolts, fuel wood and Christmas trees shipped out of the basin annually.
At this point I have no hesitation in saying that one of the largest stands, and possibly the last large stand, of cedar poles on the north American continent, is to be found in the Canadian portion of the Columbia river basin. Tests by the forest products branch of the Department of Agriculture at Washington have proven that the cedar poles shipped out of the basin have the highest tensile strength of any poles shipped from Canada. That results from the fact that the trees grow in a higher climate with somewhat slower growth, and under mountainous conditions.
With respect to mineral resources, mining within the Columbia river basin portion of British Columbia has been a major industry for the past fifty years until now the average annual production of gold, silver, copper, lead, zinc, antimony, bismuth, coal, and by-products of those minerals, is well over $100 million a year. The largest non-ferrous smelter in the British commonwealth is operated at Trail by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, which also operates vast fertilizer and chemical plants.
The fish and wild life resources of the basin are plentiful. Fish are found in the rivers, lakes and streams throughout the whole of the Columbia river basin, and these are replenished by artificial rearing and stocking operations carried on by the British Columbia game commission. Fur-bearing

The Address-Mr. Herridge animals are plentiful in the district with an estimated raw fur value of about $100,000. There are some 500 fur farms at the present time in British Columbia with an annual production of $750,000 a year. A great number of these fur farms are located within this basin.
The basin supplies marvellous recreational resources and opportunities. Outdoor recreational facilities in the Columbia river basin offer the largest range of sports to satisfy the most particular as to climate, scenery, altitude, transportation and accommodations. There is no comparable region in Canada that offers such opportunities for aquatic sports, hunting, fishing, camping, mountain climbing and skiing. With reference to skiing, I want to draw to the attention of the house two particularly fine community developments within that basin. The first and oldest is the ski jump at Revelstoke on Revelstoke mountain which is the result of many years of community effort on the part of the people of Revelstoke who were interested in the sport and interested in the young people of that district. Many of the world's champions have jumped on that hill, and many world records have been made as a result of the development of that hill in Revelstoke. Then we have a later development within the last two or three years on Red mountain at Rossland where they have one of the finest ski lifts in Canada, constructed at a very considerable cost. There are excellent hills, an excellent lodge, and everything that goes to make for excellent skiing facilities, opportunities for international and inter-varsity tournaments, and so on. The ski lift has been developed as a result of the community effort of the people of Rossland and the people of Trail, with excellent co-operation from the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
With reference to navigation resources, we have the Columbia river, of which the Arrow lakes are an extension. You can travel from Grand Coulee to Revelstoke, a distance of over 300 miles. Year by year increasing numbers of American sportsmen and American fishermen seek the pleasure of new scenes and come up from Grand Coulee in their launches. Last summer they stopped on our beach and on the beaches of neighbours of mine, and thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Increasing numbers are making the trip as far north as Revelstoke. Then we have the steamer service of the C.P.R. on the Arrow lakes, passenger and freight, and the same on the Kootenay lakes. We have barge service on
the Okanagan by the C.N.R. and C.P.R., and service also on the Slocan lakes.
Then I want to bring to the attention of this house what the constituency I represent has meant to Canada through the years. Mr. J. A. Mara, member for Yale, which at that time included East and West Kootenay, speaking in this house on April 1, 1896, had this to say:
The Kootenay district contributes more per head to the general revenue than any other part of Canada ...
I challenge anyone, taking into consideration the population of the district and the total production, to show that this condition does not prevail today.

speechtext: And that was under free enterprise.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And also under the greatest co-operative development in the whole of Canada. I mention this to indicate the importance of the district, because in proceeding with my argument I want to show how Liberal and Conservative governments have overlooked the value of this district in the Canadian economy, and have neglected to defend the rights of the people of this district under certain treaties and obligations. We know this great basin extending into Canada from the United States can be developed to its fullest extent only through co-operation between these two countries. Before adjourning the debate for this evening I want to conclude my remarks at this point by quoting from a report of a committee of congress on the Columbia river and its tributaries, appointed in 1943 and 1944, to study the possibility of developing the American portion of the Columbia river basin. This is what the report had to say, in part:
From the standpoint of resources the Columbia is is the mightiest stream on the North American continent; its potential almost beyond comprehension, for nature in one of her philanthropic moods fashioned the land with such perfection as is nowhere else known.
I now move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
